blocks.text: The SAFe DevOps Practitioner exam, SDP 6.0, has 45 single-select multiple-choice questions and a 90-minute timer. The pass mark is 73%, which means 33 correct answers. These facts come from the exam study guide as it stood on 14 November 2026. Check the guide again before you sit the exam.

blocks.text: Short mocks and papers draw from each domain in proportion to the midpoint of its range in the study guide.
blocks.title: Exam domains and this pack

blocks.text:
The six exam domains are split into 22 topics: three for DevOps foundations, three for value stream mapping, and the four activities of each pipeline aspect. Every topic has its own lesson in the same shape: the idea, a worked example, the usual exam trap, a self-check, more detail, a worked case, an exercise with its solution, the facts to learn, and a note on what was verified. A lab walks one value stream from map to improvement backlog. Three closing lessons cover commonly confused terms, exam technique and final revision.

Short mocks draw 20 questions at random, weighted by domain, with 40 minutes on the clock. The five full papers, A to E, each have 45 fixed single-select questions weighted like the exam, timed at 90 minutes. Practice never shows you a question from a paper you have not opened, so each paper stays a fresh test.

Almost every question sits somewhere on one picture: four aspects, each with four activities.

If you can place a practice in the right activity, you can answer most recall questions. Learn the sixteen names in order.

lessons.title: 1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters
lessons.summary: The gap between building and running, SAFe's definition of DevOps, and the economics of small batches.

blocks.text:
In many organisations the people who build a solution and the people who run it are measured on opposite things. Development is rewarded for change. Operations is rewarded for stability. Work crosses a wall between them in large batches, releases are rare and painful, and each failure makes the next release rarer.

SAFe defines DevOps as a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support the integration, automation and collaboration needed to develop and operate a solution. It bridges the gap between those who build and those who support and maintain. Its goal is to deliver value whenever there is a business need.

Notice what the definition leaves out. DevOps is not a team, a job title or a tool.
blocks.title: The problem to be solved

blocks.text:
At Brackley Insurance, developers are praised for features shipped and operations for months without an outage. Releases happen each quarter, after a weekend of manual steps. Each painful release makes managers add another approval, and the next release is bigger still.

A DevOps reading: both groups are acting rationally against opposing goals. The fix is a shared goal, value delivered safely and often, with shared measures such as lead time and time to recover, and with automation that makes each release small and routine. A new team in the middle would add a handoff and leave the goals in conflict.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Generic answer: create a DevOps team to own deployments. SAFe answer: DevOps is a shared mindset, culture and set of technical practices across the train; a separate team is another handoff.

Generic answer: deploy less often to reduce risk. SAFe answer: deploy smaller changes more often, so each one carries less risk.

DevOps is not a tool purchase, a job title or a department.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Is DevOps a team, a role, a tool, or something else? Something else: a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support integration, automation and collaboration across those who build and those who run the solution.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Every release has a transaction cost: the effort of building, testing, approving and deploying it. Holding work back also has a cost: value that customers do not yet have, and risk that piles up unseen. When transaction costs are high, teams batch work into large releases, which makes each release slower and riskier.

Automation lowers the transaction cost, which makes smaller batches economical. Smaller batches give faster feedback, fewer defects per release and simpler recovery. That is why SAFe's DevOps aims at the ability to release whenever the business needs it, rather than at a fixed calendar.

The outcomes usually cited for DevOps are faster time to market, higher quality, lower release risk, quicker recovery and more engaged people. They come from the culture and the practices together.
blocks.title: Why small batches pay

blocks.text: A train ships a hotfix in three weeks because every change, however small, waits for the monthly change board and a manual regression run. Automating the regression suite and replacing the board with built-in checks in the pipeline brings a hotfix down to two days. The train did not work harder; the cost of each release fell.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: For each statement, say whether it fits SAFe's view of DevOps: (a) "Our DevOps engineer handles all deployments"; (b) "We release smaller changes so failures are easy to find"; (c) "Operations joins exploration to describe how the service runs"; (d) "We bought a DevOps platform, so we are done".
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) No: a single owner is a handoff, not a shared practice. (b) Yes: small batches lower risk. (c) Yes: collaboration between building and running starts early. (d) No: DevOps is a mindset and practices, not a product.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: SAFe definition of DevOps: mindset, culture and technical practices for integration, automation and collaboration. Bridges those who build and those who run. Goal: deliver value whenever there is a business need. Transaction and holding costs; automation makes small batches economical. Not a team, title or tool.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 1.2 · The CALMR approach
lessons.summary: Culture, automation, Lean flow, measurement and recovery, with the signs of each one missing.

blocks.text:
CALMR is the mindset behind SAFe DevOps. It guides the train toward continuous value delivery through five elements.

Culture: shared responsibility for the whole value stream, and learning from failure without blame.
Automation: removing manual steps from the pipeline.
Lean flow: small batches, limits on work in process, short queues.
Measurement: data on flow, quality and value.
Recovery: designing and rehearsing for fast restoration of service.

The older industry model was CALMS, with sharing as the last letter. SAFe treats sharing as part of culture and gives the fifth place to recovery.

Two more ideas run through the course. Continuous testing means tests are automated and run all the time, not in a phase at the end. Continuous security means security practices are built into each stage.
blocks.title: CALMR

blocks.text: The element names are from the public CALMR introduction; the examples are the author's.
rows: Small batches, WIP limits, short queues
Data on flow, quality and value
Nobody knows how long a change takes
Fast rollback, fix forward, rehearsed failover
blocks.title: CALMR in practice

blocks.text:
Norrland Rail releases its ticketing system four times a year. Each release takes a weekend, and the last one was rolled back.

A CALMR reading: the culture rewards developers for features and operations for uptime, so each side protects itself. Deployments are manual, so automation is low. Four releases a year means very large batches, the opposite of lean flow. Nobody can say how long a change takes to reach customers, so measurement is missing. The rollback took nine hours, so recovery is weak.

The first step is not a tool purchase. It is to bring both groups together to map the value stream, which is the next lesson.
blocks.title: Worked example · Norrland Rail

blocks.text:
Wrong level: CALMR is the mindset behind SAFe DevOps. It is not a practice domain, a pipeline stage or a metric set.

Wrong letter: the R is recovery, not release or resilience. The older CALMS model ended with sharing, which SAFe treats as part of culture.

Culture comes first because tools alone do not change behaviour.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A train reviews deployment frequency, lead time and time to recover each iteration. Which CALMR element is this? Measurement.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
The elements reinforce each other. Automation makes small batches cheap, which supports Lean flow. Lean flow makes problems small and visible, which helps recovery. Measurement shows where flow is blocked and whether changes helped. Culture lets people report problems openly, so the measures are honest and recovery improves.

Two more ideas run through the course. Continuous testing means tests are automated and run all the time, not in a phase at the end. Continuous security means security practices are built into every stage.
blocks.title: How the elements depend on each other

blocks.text: After an outage, a manager asks who pushed the change. Next month, engineers hide a near-miss to avoid the same treatment, and a similar fault causes a longer outage. A blameless review would have found the gap in the pipeline the first time. Culture failed first; recovery failed as a result.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the CALMR element each improvement targets: (a) a one-click rollback; (b) WIP limits on the team board; (c) a shared dashboard of lead time; (d) replacing manual test runs with a pipeline stage; (e) blameless post-incident reviews.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Recovery. (b) Lean flow. (c) Measurement. (d) Automation. (e) Culture.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: CALMR: culture, automation, Lean flow, measurement, recovery. Recovery replaced sharing; sharing sits in culture. CALMR is the mindset; it guides the practice domains. Outcomes include faster time to market, fewer defects and better mean time to recover.

lessons.title: 1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security
lessons.summary: Four aspects and sixteen activities, who owns the pipeline, continuous security and the health radar.

blocks.text:
The Continuous Delivery Pipeline is the workflows, activities and automation needed to move new functionality from idea to an on-demand release of value. Each Agile Release Train builds and maintains its own pipeline, or shares one with other trains, so it can deliver value independently.

It has four aspects. Continuous Exploration works out what to build. Continuous Integration builds and validates it. Continuous Deployment moves it to production. Release on Demand makes it available to users and learns from the result. The aspects run at the same time on different work: while one feature is being explored, another is being integrated and a third is being released.
blocks.title: The pipeline at a glance

rows: Hypothesize · Collaborate and research · Architect · Synthesize
blocks.title: Four aspects, sixteen activities

blocks.text: A train at Carrow Energy draws its pipeline on a wall. Exploration is healthy, with clear hypotheses. Integration is slow: builds take an hour and fail often. Deployment is manual and monthly. Release decisions are quick, but nobody measures results. The train now knows where to look first: the build and the deployment activities, which hold back everything after them.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
The aspects are not phases done one after another for the whole solution; they run in parallel on a flow of features.

Deployment comes before release. Continuous Deployment ends with the change in production and available for release; Release on Demand decides when users get it.

Security is not a final gate. It is built into every aspect.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which aspect contains the verify activity? Continuous Deployment: deploy, verify, monitor, respond.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Continuous security, often called DevSecOps, moves security work into each activity: threat modelling while architecting, secure coding and dependency scanning while developing and building, security tests end to end, and monitoring for threats once the solution is live. Finding a flaw early costs far less than finding it after release.

SAFe's DevOps health radar is a self-assessment that scores each of the sixteen activities, so a train can see which parts of its pipeline are weakest and choose where to improve first. It describes the pipeline, not individual people.
blocks.title: Continuous security and the health radar

blocks.text: A security review before each release finds problems that take weeks to fix, so releases slip. The train adds dependency scanning to the build, a threat-modelling step to feature exploration, and automated security tests to the pipeline. The pre-release review now confirms rather than discovers, and releases stop slipping.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Place each in its aspect: (a) stage; (b) synthesize; (c) stabilize; (d) respond; (e) build; (f) measure.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Continuous Integration. (b) Continuous Exploration. (c) Release on Demand. (d) Continuous Deployment. (e) Continuous Integration. (f) Release on Demand.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Four aspects, four activities each; learn the sixteen in order. Each ART builds and maintains its pipeline. Aspects run in parallel. Continuous security and continuous testing run through every aspect. The DevOps health radar scores the sixteen activities.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 2.1 · Mapping the current value stream
lessons.summary: Why map, who maps, and how a mapping session records each step from trigger to value.

blocks.text:
A value stream is the series of steps that turns a trigger, such as a customer request, into delivered value. Mapping it makes the steps, handoffs and delays visible to everyone at once. The map describes the system. It is not a tool for rating people or teams.

The people who do the work build the map together: business, product, development, testing, security and operations. A map drawn by one group misses the delays that happen before and after its own steps.
blocks.title: Why map

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of value stream mapping; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: One trigger, such as a feature request, and the value it ends in
Everyone who touches the work, from business to operations
Map how work really flows today, not the official process
Process time, lead time, percent complete and accurate
Delays and queues between steps, and where rework comes back
Total process time, total lead time, flow efficiency, rolled accuracy
blocks.title: A mapping session, step by step

blocks.text: A train at Lindqvist Telecom maps its path from a customer request to a change in production. Product, development, testing, security and operations staff stand at one wall with sticky notes and real dates from recent work items. Security reveals a two-week wait for a review that the developers did not know existed. Nobody in the room could have drawn that step alone.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Mapping is done by the people who do the work, not by managers alone or an outside consultant.

Map the current state first, as it is, before designing the future. Mapping the official process hides the real delays.

Map from the customer's point of view: from the trigger to delivered value, not just one team's part.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Why bring real recent work items to a mapping session? Because real dates show the actual lead times and waits; memory and the official process understate them.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
A good map shows the flow, not the organisation chart. Each step has three numbers: process time, the hands-on time; lead time, the elapsed time including waiting; and percent complete and accurate, the share of output the next step can use without rework. Between the steps sit the waits, and arrows mark where work goes back for rework.

Keep the map at a level the group can see at once, usually five to fifteen steps. Too much detail hides the big delays; too little hides the handoffs. The map belongs to the people who drew it, and it is revisited as the stream changes.
blocks.title: What a good map shows

blocks.text: A team maps only its own development steps and finds them efficient. When the whole train maps from customer request to release, the development steps turn out to be under a fifth of the lead time; most of it is waiting for approvals and environments. The scope of the map decided what could be seen.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: List who should attend a session to map the path from a customer's feature request to its release in a regulated bank.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Product Management and the business, the teams who develop and test, architects, security, compliance, operations and release staff, and someone who hears from customers, such as support. Anyone whose step or approval the work passes through.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Value stream: steps from trigger to value. Map the current state with the people who do the work, from the customer's view. Three measures per step: process time, lead time, percent complete and accurate. Waits between steps. The map describes the system, not people's performance.

lessons.title: 2.2 · Value stream metrics and flow metrics
lessons.summary: Totals on the map, flow efficiency, rolled accuracy, the six flow metrics and Measure and Grow.

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of value stream mapping; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Time someone is actively working on the item
Elapsed time for the step, including waiting
Share of output the next step can use without rework
blocks.title: Three measures on each step

blocks.text:
Add the process times and the lead times along the stream. Process time divided by lead time is the activity ratio, which SAFe's flow metrics call flow efficiency: time in value-adding work divided by total flow time. In most organisations it is surprisingly low, because work waits far longer than it is worked on.

Multiply the percent complete and accurate values to get the rolled value. Three steps at 80, 50 and 50 percent give 20 percent: only one item in five passes through without rework.

The largest improvement usually sits in the delays between steps. After the current state is understood, the group designs a future state and an improvement backlog.
blocks.title: Reading the totals

blocks.text:
Calder Freight maps the path of a feature. Development takes 5 days of work inside 12 days elapsed. Testing takes 2 days of work, after 11 days waiting for an environment. Deployment takes half a day of work, after 20 days waiting for a monthly window.

Total process time is 7.5 days and total lead time is 45.5 days, so flow efficiency is about 16 percent. Making developers faster would touch 5 days. Removing the wait for an environment and the monthly window would touch 31. The improvement backlog starts with self-service environments and automated deployment.
blocks.title: Worked example · Calder Freight

blocks.text:
Flow load counts items in progress; flow velocity counts items finished. Rising load with flat velocity means longer flow time.

Percent complete and accurate is about the quality of the handoff, not progress against scope.

Flow efficiency is low in most organisations because work waits far longer than it is worked on. The fix is usually the waits, not faster working.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Three steps have percent complete and accurate of 90, 50 and 80 percent. What is the rolled value? 0.9 × 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.36, so 36 percent of items pass through without rework.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
SAFe names six flow metrics. Flow time is the time from start to completion of an item. Flow velocity is the number of items completed in a period. Flow load is the number of items in progress. Flow efficiency is active time divided by total flow time. Flow distribution is the mix of item types. Flow predictability is how consistently commitments are met.

Measure and Grow uses three measurement domains: outcomes, flow and competency. Outcomes ask whether solutions meet customer and business needs. Flow asks how efficiently value is delivered. Competency asks how proficient the organisation is in the practices.
blocks.title: Flow metrics and Measure and Grow

rows: Are we balancing features, enablers, defects and debt?
Start to completion of an item
Items in progress, active or waiting
Active time over total flow time
How much of the time is spent waiting?
Do we deliver what we commit to?
blocks.title: The six flow metrics

blocks.text: A train's flow velocity is flat, but its flow load has doubled since the last PI because new work starts before old work finishes. Flow time rises accordingly. The train stops starting and starts finishing: WIP limits on the ART backlog bring the load down, and flow time follows within a PI.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: A stream has three steps. Design: 2 days of work in 6 elapsed, 80% accurate. Build: 4 days in 10, 75% accurate. Approval: 0.5 days in 14, 100% accurate. Find total process time, total lead time, flow efficiency and rolled accuracy.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Process time 6.5 days; lead time 30 days; flow efficiency 6.5 / 30, about 22 percent. Rolled accuracy 0.8 × 0.75 × 1.0 = 60 percent. The approval step has the longest wait, 13.5 days, and is the first place to look.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Total process time and lead time; flow efficiency = process time / lead time; rolled percent complete and accurate = product of the steps. Six flow metrics: distribution, velocity, time, load, efficiency, predictability. Measure and Grow: outcomes, flow, competency.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 2.3 · From the map to improvements
lessons.summary: The future-state map, the improvement backlog, targeting the constraint and checking the results.

blocks.text:
A map is only useful if it changes the work. After the current state is understood, the same group designs a future state: the improved flow it will aim for, with fewer handoffs, shorter waits and less rework. The gap between the two becomes an improvement backlog.

Improvement items are planned like any other work. Most are enablers, such as self-service environments, automated tests or automated deployment, and they compete for capacity in the backlog using WSJF. Putting them in the backlog makes sure they are done rather than hoped for.
blocks.title: From current state to future state

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Agree examples and tests before development
blocks.title: Common findings and typical improvements

blocks.text: Calder Freight's map shows 31 of its 45.5 days lead time are waits for an environment and a monthly window. The future-state map shows environments on demand and deployment on each merge. The improvement backlog gets two enablers, scored with WSJF. A PI later, the train maps again: lead time is 16 days, and the next constraint is code review.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Start where the map shows the biggest delay, the constraint, not where the work is most visible or where a team is easiest to blame.

Adding people to a slow step rarely helps; the wait often lies elsewhere, and new people add handoffs.

Improvement work goes in the backlog and gets capacity; it is not done in spare time.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Why focus on the biggest constraint first? Because the whole stream cannot flow faster than its slowest point; improving elsewhere moves the queue without shortening lead time.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Each improvement is a hypothesis: "self-service environments will cut test waits from eleven days to one". Measure the result with the same numbers used on the map, lead time and flow efficiency for the stream, and flow time and flow load for the train. Then map again. The constraint moves, and the next round of improvements starts from the new picture.
blocks.title: Checking that the improvements worked

blocks.text: A train buys a new pipeline tool, then celebrates the number of teams using it. Lead time has not changed. A second mapping session shows the real wait is a weekly approval meeting the tool cannot touch. Results, not activity, show whether an improvement worked.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: A map shows: development 3 days of work in 5 elapsed; waiting for security review 10 days; deployment 1 day of work in 2 elapsed. Write one improvement backlog item and its measure.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: "Build automated security checks into the pipeline and limit manual review to high-risk changes. Measure: wait for security review falls from 10 days to under 1 day, and total lead time from 17 days to under 8."
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Future-state map; improvement backlog of enablers ranked by WSJF; target the constraint; measure with lead time and flow efficiency; remap regularly. Theory of constraints: the slowest point sets the pace.

lessons.title: Lab · Map a value stream and plan the fixes
lessons.summary: One feature's path at Fenwick Water, from request to release: the map, the totals, the constraint and the backlog.

blocks.text: Fenwick Water wants to know why a small change to its billing portal takes two months to reach customers. A mapping session brings together product, two development teams, testing, security, operations and the change manager. They trace five recent changes from request to release and agree average figures for each step.
blocks.title: The brief

rows: Wait for test environment, then test
blocks.title: Step 1 · The current-state map

blocks.text: Total process time: 1 + 4 + 2 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 8 days. Total lead time: 8 + 9 + 14 + 10 + 16 = 57 days. Flow efficiency: 8 / 57, about 14 percent. Rolled accuracy: 0.7 × 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.95 × 1.0, about 48 percent, so roughly half of all changes go back for rework at least once.
blocks.title: Step 2 · The totals

blocks.text: The largest waits are the change board and deployment (15.5 days of waiting), the test environment (12 days) and security review (9.5 days). Development, the step everyone first suspected, has only 5 days of waiting. Refinement's 70 percent accuracy explains much of the rework: unclear requests come back from test.
blocks.title: Step 3 · Find the constraint

rows: Test step lead time under 3 days
blocks.title: Step 4 · The improvement backlog

blocks.text: Each item is an enabler with a cost of delay and a size. Automated deployment removes the largest wait and helps every later change, so it scores highest on WSJF despite its size. The train plans it in the next PI, measures the deploy wait each iteration, and books a second mapping session for the following PI, when a new constraint will have appeared.
blocks.title: Step 5 · Rank and plan

blocks.text: Map with everyone, add up the numbers, find the biggest wait, turn the gap into ranked enablers, measure, and map again.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Hypothesize
lessons.summary: Why ideas start as hypotheses, how to write one, MVPs, leading indicators and pivot or persevere.

blocks.text:
Continuous Exploration is the first aspect of the pipeline and the largest exam domain. It drives innovation and alignment on what to build by continually exploring market and customer needs, and it produces a vision, a roadmap and a set of features in the ART Backlog. Product Management prioritises those features.

It replaces a large up-front requirements phase with a steady flow of small features. Every idea is treated as a hypothesis until evidence supports it.
blocks.title: What exploration is for

blocks.text: The activity names follow the topic list in the study guide; the descriptions are the author's.
rows: State the expected, measurable benefit and how it will be tested
Work with customers and stakeholders to understand needs
Shape the solution so it can be delivered continuously
Turn the result into a vision, roadmap and prioritised features
blocks.title: The four activities

blocks.text:
A good benefit hypothesis names the change, who it is for, and the measurable result that would show it worked. One common shape is: "We believe that [this outcome] will be achieved if [these users] get [this benefit] from [this feature]. We will know we are right when [this measure] moves by [this much]."

The measure has two parts. A leading indicator moves early, during an MVP or soon after release, and predicts the outcome: weekly use of a new page, the share of bookings made online. A lagging outcome, such as revenue or retention, arrives later and confirms the value. Leading indicators let the train decide before the lagging result arrives.

Measures are agreed before work starts, by Product Management with the business. Measures picked afterwards tend to be the ones that look good.
blocks.title: Writing a hypothesis

blocks.text:
Solace Health believes online booking will cut missed appointments. The hypothesis: clinics using the new flow will see missed appointments fall by a fifth within three months. The leading indicator is the share of bookings made online each week.

Product Management visits three clinics and watches reception staff. Architects decide the booking service must be deployable on its own and hidden behind a toggle. The feature set is written with benefit hypotheses, scored with WSJF and brought to PI Planning. If clinics do not use the flow, the result is a pivot, not a larger budget.
blocks.title: Worked example · Solace Health

blocks.text:
Generic answer: a customer request is a requirement. SAFe answer: it is a hypothesis to validate.

Generic answer: the MVP is the smallest sellable release. SAFe answer: it is the smallest thing that tests the hypothesis's riskiest assumptions.

A plan ("we will build X next PI") or a claim about the past ("customers have always wanted X") is not a hypothesis: neither can be tested.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: An MVP shows high usage but flat revenue. Persevere, pivot or stop? Neither success nor failure yet: refine the hypothesis about why usage does not turn into revenue, and test that cheaply.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
A benefit hypothesis is the proposed measurable benefit of an epic, capability, feature or story. For a large initiative, a Minimum Viable Product is an early and minimal version used to prove or disprove the epic hypothesis. Lean startup thinking then asks for a decision: persevere, pivot or stop. Innovation accounting supplies the leading indicators that make that decision possible before financial results arrive.

Research is primary when you gather evidence first-hand, for example by watching users work, and secondary when you rely on reports and data collected by others. Lean UX keeps the design loop short by focusing on iterative learning and customer outcomes.
blocks.title: Hypothesize, then research

blocks.text: A Business Owner is certain a feature will succeed and wants no measures. Product Management agrees a leading indicator anyway. Three weeks after release, usage is a third of the forecast, and a small change to the entry point doubles it. Without the measure, nobody would have looked.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Rewrite as a testable hypothesis: "Build a mobile app for meter readings."
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: "We believe customers who submit meter readings in the app will make fewer estimated-bill complaints. We will know we are right when 30% of readings come through the app within two months (leading) and estimated-bill complaints fall by a fifth within six months (lagging)."
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Every idea is a hypothesis. Benefit hypothesis with measures agreed up front. Leading indicators steer; lagging outcomes confirm. MVP tests the riskiest assumptions cheaply. Build, measure, learn. Persevere, pivot or stop. Innovation accounting. A disproved hypothesis frees capacity.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Collaborate and research
lessons.summary: Who joins exploration, primary and secondary research, and the design thinking tools that keep users in view.

blocks.text:
Collaborate and research brings together the people who understand the need and the people who will build and run the answer: customers, Product Management, Business Owners, the System Architect, teams, and the operations and support staff who know how the solution behaves in production. Subject-matter experts join when a feature touches their domain, such as billing rules or regulation.

Research runs all the time, alongside delivery, because markets and needs change and insight goes stale. Its output is understanding: what users need, in what context, which feeds the architect and synthesize activities.
blocks.title: Who explores, and why

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of design thinking and Lean UX.
rows: Observation at the place of work (gemba)
Real workarounds and context users rarely mention
Breadth and trends, often secondary data
A realistic picture of a type of user, built from research
What a user says, thinks, does and feels
Each step a customer takes, with feelings and pain points
How released features are really used
blocks.title: Research tools and what they give

blocks.text: A product manager at Holt Utilities is sure customers want a chat assistant. Before writing any feature, the team spends two days in the call centre and listens to calls. Most calls are about one confusing line on the bill. The first hypothesis becomes a clearer bill, tested with a sample of customers, and the chat assistant waits.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Opinions, however senior, are hypotheses. Research tests them before money is spent.

A survey of only the happiest customers is a biased sample; it hides the needs of those who might leave.

Research is not a one-off phase before a project; it is continuous.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is the difference between primary and secondary research? Primary research gathers new data first-hand, such as interviews or observation; secondary research uses data others collected, such as market reports.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Good research separates what users say from what they do. Observation and telemetry show behaviour; interviews explain it. When research shows two user groups need different things, exploration produces separate hypotheses for each, rather than one averaged feature that suits neither.

Distributed teams can still do first-hand research through remote interviews and watching users share their screens. Architects and operations staff take part because technical options and constraints shape what is feasible, and because operations hears from users every day.
blocks.title: Research that shapes the solution

blocks.text: A train designs a new claims form from internal workshops alone. After release, completion rates fall. Watching five customers try the form shows that a required field asks for a number most customers do not have to hand. One afternoon of observation earlier would have saved a release.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Pick the best tool: (a) understand a nurse's shift before designing a ward app; (b) see how a released feature is used; (c) summarise a type of user for the whole team; (d) see where customers get frustrated while switching tariff.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Observation at the place of work. (b) Production telemetry. (c) A persona. (d) A customer journey map.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Collaborators: customers, Product Management, Business Owners, architects, teams, operations, support, subject-matter experts. Primary versus secondary research. Gemba. Personas, empathy maps, journey maps. Research is continuous. Separate hypotheses for different groups. Representative samples.

lessons.title: 3.3 · Architect
lessons.summary: Designing for continuous delivery: releasability, testability, operability, security, runway and enablers.

blocks.text:
The pipeline can only flow if the solution is designed for it. The Architectural Runway is the existing code, components and technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features with minimal redesign. Emergent design alone does not scale, so SAFe balances it with intentional architecture. Enablers pave the runway and come in four types: exploration, architecture, infrastructure and compliance.

Architects design for releasability, so that deployment can be separated from release, for testability, for operations and for security. Threat modelling belongs here, before code exists. Nonfunctional requirements are system qualities that constrain the backlogs and are revisited with the definition of done.
blocks.title: Architect for continuous delivery

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Feature toggles; backward-compatible changes; separately deployable parts
Seams for test doubles; automated test hooks; production-like test environments
Built-in logs, metrics and traces; health checks
Threat modelling before code; least privilege; secrets kept out of code
Redundancy, failover, blue-green or canary support
blocks.title: Design for each quality

blocks.text: A new pricing engine must be deployed weeks before a marketing launch. The System Architect designs it to run beside the old engine behind a toggle, with telemetry comparing their results on real traffic. The team can deploy early, verify in production, and leave the release decision to the business.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Designing for separate deployment and release is an exploration decision, made by architects, not something bolted on at deployment time.

NFRs shape the architecture, which is costly to change, so they are considered in exploration rather than added before release.

Enablers are not overhead to be scheduled last; they compete on WSJF like everything else.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which enabler type fits a short investigation of a data store nobody has used? An exploration enabler, such as a spike or prototype.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

rows: Knowledge, through research, prototypes and spikes
The technical runway of the solution
blocks.title: Four kinds of enabler

blocks.text: A train's runway is nearly used up: each new feature needs changes to a shared database schema. Exploration plans an architectural enabler to split the schema by domain, a PI ahead of the features that need it. Incident and capacity data from operations shows which part to split first.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Classify each enabler: (a) build self-service test environments; (b) a three-day spike on a message broker; (c) add the audit logging a regulator requires; (d) extract a shared payments service that the next five features need.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Infrastructure. (b) Exploration. (c) Compliance. (d) Architectural.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Architect for releasability, testability, operability, security and recovery. Architectural runway: existing code, components and infrastructure for near-term features. Emergent design balanced with intentional architecture. Four enabler types. NFRs are system qualities that constrain the backlogs. Threat modelling before code. Spikes test options cheaply.

lessons.title: 3.4 · Synthesize
lessons.summary: Vision, roadmap, features ready for PI Planning, WSJF and the ART backlog as a Kanban system.

blocks.text:
A feature delivers business value and fits in one planning interval for one train. It carries a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria. The backlog is sequenced by Weighted Shortest Job First: cost of delay divided by job size. Cost of delay adds user and business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement.

WSJF applies to the whole backlog. A pipeline enabler that removes delay from every later feature can outrank a customer feature.
blocks.title: Synthesize and prioritise

blocks.text: Relative scores, as used in SAFe's WSJF; the items are invented.
blocks.title: WSJF worked through

blocks.text: The enabler outranks both features: its cost of delay is the highest because every later feature waits on slow deployments, and it is small. Feature C has the highest user-business value but is large, so it comes last. If C can be split, the most valuable slice may move up.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Wrong role: Product Management owns and prioritises the ART backlog; the Product Owner owns the team backlog; the RTE facilitates the train.

WSJF divides cost of delay by job size, not the other way round. Time criticality is part of cost of delay, not the denominator.

A feature too big for one PI is split into smaller features that each deliver value, not into technical tasks by layer.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Feature A has cost of delay 20 and size 5; feature B has 30 and 10. Which first? A: 20 / 5 = 4 beats 30 / 10 = 3.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Synthesize turns what was learned and designed into a vision, a roadmap and prioritised features. The vision describes the future state of the solution and why it matters. The roadmap forecasts deliverables and milestones over the next few PIs. Features in the ART backlog each have a short name, a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria, and fit in one PI.

The ART backlog is managed as a Kanban system, which makes the flow of features visible and limits work in each state, so exploration keeps pace with delivery capacity. Product Management ranks first and refines only the top items with the teams; refining fifty features for one PI's capacity wastes effort. Capacity allocation reserves a share for enablers, maintenance and debt.
blocks.title: From exploration to PI Planning

blocks.text: Before PI Planning, a train's top features have no acceptance criteria, and teams spend half of the first day asking what they mean. For the next PI, Product Management holds refinement sessions with the teams in the last two iterations. The top ten features arrive with hypotheses and criteria, and planning finishes on time.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Rank by WSJF: X has cost of delay 12 and size 3; Y has 20 and 8; Z has 9 and 2.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Z = 4.5, X = 4.0, Y = 2.5. Order: Z, X, Y. Y has the highest cost of delay but is the largest job.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Outputs: vision, roadmap, prioritised ART backlog. Feature: name, benefit hypothesis, acceptance criteria, fits in a PI. WSJF = cost of delay / job size; cost of delay = user-business value + time criticality + risk reduction or opportunity enablement. ART backlog as a Kanban system. Capacity allocation. Product Management owns the ART backlog.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Develop
lessons.summary: Turning stories into tested code: test-first, small stories, version control, pairing and secure coding.

blocks.text:
Continuous Integration is the aspect of the pipeline where new functionality is developed, tested, integrated and validated in preparation for deployment and release. The aim is a system that is always running and potentially deployable, even in the middle of development.

It has four activities. Develop implements stories and commits code and components to version control. Build creates deployable binaries and merges development branches into the trunk. Test end-to-end validates the solution. Stage hosts and validates it in a staging environment before production.
blocks.title: What integration is for

blocks.text: The activity names are from the public article; the practices are written from the author's knowledge.
rows: Small stories, TDD, BDD, version control, built-in quality
Trunk-based development, gated commits, build automation, security scanning
Test automation, production-like environments, test data, service virtualisation, NFR testing
Staging environment, blue-green deployment, System Demo
blocks.title: Practices by activity

blocks.text:
Test-Driven Development builds and runs a test before the code it checks. Behavior-Driven Development defines business-facing scenarios before or with the specification of behaviour, and needs three perspectives: customer, development and test. Both are test-first practices. Together they produce many fast automated tests and few slow end-to-end ones.

Quality is the whole team's job. Agile testing is collaborative, and tests are automated wherever possible.
blocks.title: Test-first

blocks.text: A team splits a new payments feature into four stories, each finishable within an iteration. For each, the team agrees BDD scenarios with the Product Owner, then a pair writes unit tests before the code. Unfinished work is merged to the main branch at least daily, hidden behind a feature toggle. Nothing waits on a long-lived branch.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
TDD versus BDD: TDD is the developer cycle on units of code; BDD is shared, business-facing behaviour agreed by customer, development and test perspectives.

Wrong activity: merging to the trunk is build, not develop.

Testers do not own quality; the whole team does. Tests written after the code, or by someone else, lose the test-first benefit.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A developer finishes the code for a story but has written no tests. What is wrong under test-first? Tests should have shaped the code from the start; writing them later loses their effect on design.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Everything needed to build and run the solution lives in version control: code, tests, configuration and infrastructure definitions. Developers commit small changes to the shared main branch at least daily, so each change is small and conflicts surface early. Pairing and code review catch problems early and spread knowledge; they complement automated tests rather than replacing them.

Security is built in while coding: secure coding practices and early checks catch vulnerabilities when they are cheapest to fix. Self-service, disposable environments remove waits for shared test databases.
blocks.title: Habits of the develop activity

blocks.text: Developers wait two days for a shared test database, so they batch several stories before testing. The train provides disposable environments created from code on demand. Stories are tested as they are written, and the batch disappears.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Which practice fits: (a) keep unfinished work in the main branch safely; (b) catch a design flaw before merge and share knowledge; (c) make a build reproducible; (d) catch a vulnerability while coding?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) A feature toggle. (b) Pairing or code review. (c) Everything in version control, with pinned dependencies. (d) Secure coding practice and early security checks.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Develop: split features into stories; TDD and BDD; version control for everything; commit at least daily; pairing and review; toggles for unfinished work; built-in quality; secure coding. Stories fit in an iteration.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Build
lessons.summary: Trunk-based development, gated commits, fast automated builds, build once deploy many, and security scanning.

blocks.text: Build creates deployable binaries and merges development branches into the trunk. Every commit triggers an automated build and fast tests, so a failure points to one small change. The main branch is kept working at all times: when it breaks, fixing or reverting it comes before anything else, because every team builds on it.
blocks.title: What build does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Small changes merged often, so conflicts stay small
A change reaches the main line only if the build and tests pass
Feedback on every commit, in minutes
The artefact tested is the artefact deployed
Code flaws and vulnerable libraries found early
The same result on any machine
blocks.title: Build practices

blocks.text:
# Illustrative pipeline definition. It is displayed here, not run.
trigger:
  branches: [main]            # trunk-based: every merge to main starts the pipeline

stages:
  - stage: Build              # CI: build
    steps:
      - script: dotnet build --configuration Release
      - script: dotnet test tests/Unit        # fast developer tests
      - script: security-scan ./src           # static analysis on each commit
  - stage: TestEndToEnd       # CI: test end-to-end
    steps:
      - script: deploy --env test --version $(Build.Id)
      - script: dotnet test tests/Acceptance  # BDD scenarios, virtualised partners
  - stage: Stage              # CI: stage
    steps:
      - script: deploy --env staging --slot green --version $(Build.Id)
  - stage: Deploy             # CD: deploy and verify
    steps:
      - script: deploy --env production --toggles off --version $(Build.Id)
      - script: dotnet test tests/Smoke --env production
blocks.title: A short pipeline example

blocks.text:
Teams at Farrow Systems keep feature branches for three weeks. Merges fail, and the main line is broken for days before each System Demo.

The train moves to short-lived branches merged daily, with a gated commit that runs the build and unit tests before a change reaches the trunk. A partner's payment service is rarely available in test, so the team virtualises it. The staging environment is rebuilt from the same definitions as production, and the System Demo runs from staging each iteration.
blocks.title: Worked example · Farrow Systems

blocks.text:
Running the build once a night instead of on each commit delays feedback and mixes many changes into one failure.

Rebuilding the artefact for each environment risks deploying something other than what was tested.

A broken main line is not left for its author to fix later; it blocks every team.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is a gated commit? A change that merges to the main line only if the build and tests pass, so the shared branch stays working.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A build takes forty minutes, so developers stop running it before committing, and the main line breaks twice a week. The team caches dependencies, runs tests in parallel and moves slow suites to a later stage. The commit build drops to six minutes, developers run it again, and breaks become rare.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the practice: (a) one container image moves from test to staging to production; (b) a scan flags a library with a known vulnerability; (c) everyone merges small changes to one branch several times a day.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Build once, deploy many. (b) Software composition analysis. (c) Trunk-based development.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Build: deployable binaries; merge to trunk. Trunk-based development; gated commits; build on every commit; fast builds; fix a broken main line at once; build once, deploy many; versioned artefacts; static and composition analysis. System-level integration of all teams' work, not just each team's.

lessons.title: 4.3 · Test end-to-end
lessons.summary: Validating the integrated solution: automation, the test pyramid, test data, service virtualisation and NFRs.

blocks.text:
Test end-to-end validates the integrated solution as a whole, functional behaviour and nonfunctional requirements, in an environment as close to production as possible. Its job is to find what team-level tests cannot: problems in how the parts work together.

Tests are automated and run continuously as changes arrive, not in a phase at the end of the PI. Most checks stay in fast unit and service tests, with a smaller number of end-to-end journeys, which keeps the pipeline quick and reliable.
blocks.title: What test end-to-end does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of the test pyramid and agile testing.
blocks.title: Kinds of test and where they sit

blocks.text: A partner's payment service is rarely available in test, so end-to-end tests fail at random. The team adds service virtualisation: a stand-in that behaves like the partner for agreed scenarios. Tests become reliable, and a contract test checks that the stand-in still matches the real service.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Rerunning flaky tests until they pass hides real defects; find and fix the causes, such as timing, shared data or unstable environments.

End-to-end tests should be fewer than unit tests; they are slower and more brittle.

Testing on a copy of live customer data creates privacy risk; use realistic, anonymised data.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Why run end-to-end tests in a production-like environment? Differences from production in versions, configuration or data hide defects until release.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Test data management provides realistic, anonymised data created or refreshed on demand, so each run starts clean. Environments are built from the same code as production. Nonfunctional requirements, such as response time under load or resistance to common attacks, are tested continuously, because any change can break them.

Automated regression runs on every change, so breakage is found soon after the change that caused it. Exploratory testing still has a place for finding new kinds of problem in new work.
blocks.title: Data, environments and nonfunctional tests

blocks.text: A train runs its full regression suite once, at the end of each PI, and spends the last iteration fixing what it finds. It automates the suite and runs it nightly, then on each merge. Defects are found within hours of being introduced, and the end-of-PI crunch disappears.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Which practice helps: (a) a partner system is costly to call in test; (b) tests fail when two teams use the same records; (c) a change slows checkout under load?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Service virtualisation. (b) Test data created on demand for each run. (c) Continuous nonfunctional (performance) testing.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Test end-to-end: the integrated solution, functional and nonfunctional, in a production-like environment. Test automation; test pyramid; regression on every change; test data management; service virtualisation; NFR testing; fix flaky tests. Quality is the whole team's job.

lessons.title: 4.4 · Stage
lessons.summary: Hosting and validating in staging: production-like environments from code, blue-green, and the System Demo.

blocks.text:
Stage hosts and validates the solution in a staging environment before production. Staging is the last high-confidence check, so it must behave like production: same versions, same configuration, same infrastructure definitions. A successful run there is real evidence only if the environments match.

The integrated increment of the whole train is often shown from staging at the System Demo each iteration, so stakeholders see real, working progress rather than slides.
blocks.title: What stage does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Staging built from infrastructure as code
An environment that mirrors production and can be rebuilt exactly
Staging on demand, even one per feature
A rehearsal of the production switch
Stakeholders see the integrated system each iteration
blocks.title: Stage practices

blocks.text: A train's staging environment runs an older database version than production, and two releases fail in production on queries that passed in staging. The train rebuilds staging from the same infrastructure code as production and destroys and recreates it each week. The next five releases behave in production exactly as they did in staging.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Wrong activity: hosting in a production-like environment is stage, part of Continuous Integration; deploy, the first activity of Continuous Deployment, moves the change to production.

Wrong event: the integrated work of the whole train is shown at the System Demo each iteration, not only at Inspect and Adapt.

Staging is not a backup or a spare for production.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which activity follows test end-to-end? Stage, the last activity of Continuous Integration.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
When staging can be created and destroyed automatically, it stops being a scarce shared resource with a booking calendar. Teams validate each change in a realistic setting without waiting, and the operations team no longer handles queues of environment requests.

Staging does not replace monitoring in production. Some problems appear only with real traffic, which is why Continuous Deployment still verifies and monitors after each deployment.
blocks.title: Why staging matters for flow

blocks.text: Teams book a single staging environment through a spreadsheet, and features wait a week for a slot. The train automates provisioning from versioned configuration, so each feature branch can have its own short-lived staging environment. The booking spreadsheet is retired.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Is each statement true or false? (a) Staging should be rebuilt from the same code as production. (b) Passing in staging removes the need to verify in production. (c) The System Demo can run from staging.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) True. (b) False: verify still runs after deployment. (c) True.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Stage: host and validate in a staging environment before production. Production-like through infrastructure as code. Automated provisioning. Blue-green rehearsal. System Demo each iteration, often from staging. Stage is the last CI activity; deploy starts CD.

lessons.title: 5.1 · Deploy
lessons.summary: Moving validated changes to production: automation, toggles, dark launches, blue-green and safe database changes.

blocks.text:
Continuous Deployment is the aspect of the pipeline that automates the migration of new functionality from a staging environment to production, where it is made available for release. Deployment is a technical event. Release is a business decision. Keeping them apart is the central idea of this domain.

When deployment is separate from release, changes reach production without altering what users see. That allows functionality to be shown to chosen customers, experiments such as A/B tests, small batches, and release when the business wants it. Automation lowers the transaction cost of each deployment, which is what makes small batches economical.
blocks.title: What deployment is for

blocks.text: Activity names and meanings are from the public article; the practices are written from the author's knowledge.
rows: Deployment automation, feature toggles, dark launches, selective and self-service deployment
Confirm it works in production before customers see it
Production testing, test automation, NFR tests
Watch production and report on issues
Proactive detection, rollback and fix forward, immutable infrastructure, blameless reviews
blocks.title: The four activities

blocks.text:
A feature toggle hides deployed code until it is switched on. A dark launch runs functionality in production without users seeing it. A canary release shows a change to a small share of real users and widens gradually; it is a release technique. Blue-green deployment keeps two production environments and switches traffic between them.

When something fails, restoring service comes first. Roll back when that is fastest and safe; fix forward when a fix is quicker or rollback is not possible.
blocks.title: Techniques that are easy to confuse

blocks.text: A team deploys by running scripts by hand from a checklist, once a month, with a two-hour outage. It automates the deployment through the pipeline and adopts blue-green: the new version starts beside the old, smoke tests run, and traffic switches over. Outages disappear, rollback is a switch back, and deployment moves to every merge.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Generic answer: deployed means released. SAFe answer: deployed means in production and available for release.

A change board that approves each deployment adds delay and little information. Automation and verification provide the control.

Deploying less often to cut manual effort makes each deployment bigger and riskier; automate instead.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is a dark launch? Running functionality in production, for example with real traffic, without users seeing it.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Small, frequent deployments lower risk because each changes little: if something fails, the cause is obvious and rollback is easy. Teams deploy through a self-service pipeline with built-in controls, rather than raising tickets for an operations queue.

Database changes need care because old and new code run side by side during a deployment. Backward-compatible changes are made in steps: add the new structure, migrate, move the code across, and only later remove the old structure. Dropping a column first would break the version still running.
blocks.title: Deploying without breaking what runs

blocks.text:
# Illustrative. Deployment puts code in production; the toggle decides who sees it.
deploy:
  environment: production
  strategy: blue-green
  toggles:
    new-pricing-engine: off        # deployed, verified, not released
verify:
  - smoke-tests --env production
  - nfr-check --latency-p95 300ms
monitor:
  alerts:
    error-rate: "> 1% for 5m -> page on-call, auto-rollback"
blocks.title: Toggle-guarded deployment

blocks.text: A feature must be in production by September but launched with a November campaign. It is deployed and verified behind a toggle in September, so the risky technical work is finished early. In November, the release is a business decision that takes seconds.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the technique: (a) two production environments, with traffic switched between them; (b) code in production, switched off; (c) a feature exercised with real traffic but invisible to users; (d) add a column, migrate, then drop the old one a release later.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Blue-green deployment. (b) A feature toggle. (c) A dark launch. (d) A backward-compatible, expand-and-contract schema change.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Deploy: move the solution to production. Deployment is technical; release is a business decision. Deployment automation; feature toggles; dark launches; selective and self-service deployment; blue-green; backward-compatible database changes. Small, frequent deployments lower risk.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Verify
lessons.summary: Confirming changes work in production before users rely on them: smoke tests, production testing and safe test data.

blocks.text:
Verify confirms that a deployed change works correctly in production before it affects users. It is the step that distinguishes Continuous Deployment's testing from the testing done in Continuous Integration: the environment is production itself.

Some problems show only with real traffic, data and configuration, so production testing complements earlier testing rather than replacing it. Verification is automated, so every deployment is checked fast and in the same way.
blocks.title: What verify does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Quick proof that the main functions work
Limited impact if a problem appears
Real use in production before customers
Synthetic or masked test data, cleaned up
Production tests without harming customers or reports
Latency and error rates within targets
blocks.title: Verify practices

blocks.text:
Garnet Travel deploys a new search service at ten in the morning with its toggle off. Smoke tests pass in production. The toggle is opened to staff, and telemetry shows response times within the agreed limit.

A later deployment raises the error rate for a tenth of users. The pipeline rolls back in two minutes. The review asks what allowed the fault through and adds a production test; it does not ask who typed the command.
blocks.title: Worked example · Garnet Travel

blocks.text:
Verify happens in production, after deployment. Validation in staging belongs to Continuous Integration.

Passing smoke tests shows the system is up; it does not show every key journey works. Cover the critical business transactions too.

Never copy real customer data into test accounts.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Verification fails right after a deployment. What next? Roll back or fix forward at once, before the change affects users.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Production tests use clearly marked synthetic or masked data and remove it afterwards, so customers and business reports are not affected. Exposing a change first to a small share of traffic, or to employees through a toggle, limits how many people a problem can reach. Testing at peak hours, or with everyone at once, maximises harm.

When verification fails, the change is not fit for users. Waiting to see whether the failure clears, or releasing to collect more data, spreads the harm.
blocks.title: Testing in production safely

blocks.text: A deployment passes its smoke tests, but business customers cannot complete a bulk transfer, a journey only one segment uses. The team adds automated checks of the critical journeys for each customer segment to its verify stage. The next similar fault is caught before the toggle opens.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Pick the practice: (a) quick checks right after deployment; (b) let staff use a feature in production before customers; (c) keep production test records out of sales reports.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Smoke tests. (b) A toggle targeted at employees. (c) Marked synthetic data, cleaned up after the test.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Verify: confirm the change works in production before users rely on it. Production testing; smoke tests; key journeys; small share of traffic; staff first; synthetic or masked data; automated verification; roll back or fix forward on failure.

lessons.title: 5.3 · Monitor
lessons.summary: Full-stack telemetry, alerts that matter, logs, metrics and traces, SLOs and business measures.

blocks.text:
Monitor watches production and reports on issues. Full-stack telemetry collects data across the infrastructure, the application and the business, so teams see both technical health and whether value is arriving. CPU and memory alone miss most of it: users can suffer while servers look healthy, and a technically perfect release can deliver no value.

Useful telemetry depends on how the code is built, so monitoring is designed in during exploration and development, not bolted on at release.
blocks.title: What monitor does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: How much and how often: latency, errors, saturation
Where a slow request spends its time across services
Is the feature used; does it change behaviour?
Is reliability within the agreed target?
blocks.title: Signals and what they answer

blocks.text: A team's dashboards raise hundreds of alerts a day, and engineers ignore them. The team keeps only alerts tied to user impact and service level objectives, each with a named action. Alerts fall to a handful a week, and the next real problem is answered in minutes.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Monitor belongs to Continuous Deployment. Stabilize, which sounds similar, belongs to Release on Demand.

More alerts do not mean better monitoring; alert fatigue hides real problems.

Server metrics do not show value. Feature usage and conversion do.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is a service level objective? A target, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding, for a measure of service reliability. It guides alerting and how much risk a team can take with changes.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Trends give early warning. Memory that climbs after each deployment, or a slowly rising error rate, can be fixed before users notice. Visual displays put the key measures where everyone can see them, so development and operations share one picture.

Monitoring also feeds the measure activity of Release on Demand: telemetry on how users use features is the evidence for or against each benefit hypothesis.
blocks.title: Seeing trends and sharing the view

blocks.text: One slow request in a chain of eight services takes hours to diagnose because each service logs separately. The team adds distributed tracing with a shared request identifier. The next slowdown is traced to one database call in ten minutes.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Which signal answers: (a) is the new search feature being used; (b) which service makes checkout slow; (c) what error did one customer hit a minute ago?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Business metrics. (b) Distributed tracing. (c) Logs, filtered by customer and time.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Monitor: watch production and report on issues. Full-stack telemetry: infrastructure, application, business. Visual displays. Logs, metrics, traces. SLOs. Alerts on user impact; avoid alert fatigue. Designed in early. Feeds the measure activity.

lessons.title: 5.4 · Respond
lessons.summary: Restoring service fast: detection, rollback and fix forward, runbooks, on-call, blameless reviews and MTTR.

blocks.text:
Respond addresses problems rapidly. Restoring service comes first, through rollback, failover or a quick fix; finding the root cause comes after. Roll back when that is fastest and safe; fix forward when a fix is quicker or rollback is not possible. A fast pipeline lets even an urgent fix go through the usual tests, which is safer than patching servers by hand.

Mean time to recover measures how quickly service is restored after a failure. It is a key DevOps measure, alongside change failure rate, which counts how often deployments cause incidents.
blocks.title: What respond does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Problems found before users report them
Replace rather than patch, so no drift
Known issues handled quickly and consistently
Someone ready to act at any time
Open accounts that reveal system causes
blocks.title: Respond practices

blocks.text: A deployment raises the error rate for a tenth of users. Monitoring pages the on-call engineer, and the pipeline rolls back in two minutes. The review asks what allowed the fault through, not who typed the command, and the fix, a new production test, goes into the backlog like any other work.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Blame first, fix later is the wrong order. Restore service, then find causes, in a blameless review.

Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable; accountability moves to fixing the system.

Manual patches on production servers cause drift and new errors; fix through the pipeline.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Why should incident findings go into the backlog? So fixes for root causes are prioritised and planned like other work rather than forgotten.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Recovery improves with practice. Runbooks record how to handle known issues and are automated over time. Chaos engineering injects controlled failures to test resilience and response before real incidents. In DevOps, the team that builds a service often shares its on-call, which motivates building it to be operable.

Fast response supports release on demand: when problems are detected and fixed quickly, the cost of a bad release falls, so the business can release more often with confidence.
blocks.title: Getting better at recovery

blocks.text: Only one customer reports a fault, and the team cannot reproduce it. Logs and telemetry filtered by that customer show a rare data combination. The fix goes out through the normal pipeline the same day; rolling back a month of releases would have been out of proportion.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Order these responses to an incident: write the review; restore service; add root-cause fixes to the backlog; detect the problem.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Detect the problem; restore service; write the blameless review; add root-cause fixes to the backlog.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Respond: address problems rapidly. Restore first, then root cause. Rollback or fix forward through the pipeline. Mean time to recover; change failure rate. lessons.title: 6.1 · Release
lessons.summary: Who decides, decoupled release elements, progressive rollout, and release governance without delay.

blocks.text:
Release on Demand is the aspect of the pipeline that releases new functionality immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs. On demand does not mean constantly. It means the business can release whenever it chooses, which for one solution is many times a day and for another is twice a year.

Product Management and the business owners decide when to release, which features, and to which users. Market rhythms and roadmap milestones inform the timing. Because release is decoupled from deployment, marketing can plan promotions and sales can schedule with confidence.
blocks.title: What release on demand means

blocks.text: The activity names follow the study guide's topic list; the practices are written from the author's knowledge.
rows: Feature toggles, canary releases, decoupled release elements
Keep the solution reliable, secure and available
Failover and disaster recovery, continuous security monitoring, architecting for operations
Compare results with the benefit hypothesis
Decide what to do next and improve the pipeline
Lean startup thinking, value stream mapping, relentless improvement
blocks.title: The four activities

blocks.text:
Halyard Retail deploys a loyalty feature in September behind a toggle. Marketing wants to launch with a November campaign, so the feature stays deployed and dark. In November it opens to two percent of customers as a canary, then to everyone.

The hypothesis was a rise in repeat purchases. After four weeks the leading indicator, the share of customers who open the loyalty page twice, has not moved. Product Management pivots the feature toward a simpler reward and records the learning as input to the next exploration cycle.
blocks.title: Worked example · Halyard Retail

blocks.text:
Generic answer: release when the code is ready. SAFe answer: release when the business needs it.

Wrong role: the Release Train Engineer and the teams make release routine; Product Management and Business Owners choose the timing.

Wrong cadence: the planning interval is a planning cadence. It does not fix when releases happen.

Monolith thinking: releasing every element together at the pace of the slowest one. SAFe decouples release elements.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Does release on demand mean every team releases daily? No. It means the business can release whenever it chooses; for one solution that is many times a day, for another twice a year.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Different parts of a solution may need different release rhythms: a mobile app, an API and a billing engine have different market needs and risks. Architecture that lets them release separately gives the business that choice.

Progressive rollout widens exposure step by step, using toggles or routing, while watching the measures; the business can pull back if needed. Release governance covers compliance, security, documentation and support readiness. In a regulated firm, the pipeline can record each build, test, approval and release automatically, which satisfies auditors without monthly approval meetings.
blocks.title: Releasing safely and in step with the business

blocks.text: A regulated firm holds a monthly meeting to approve all releases, so changes wait up to four weeks. It replaces the meeting with automated audit trails from the pipeline and pre-agreed criteria for low-risk changes. Auditors get better records, and release waits drop to days.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Who decides: (a) when a feature is released to customers; (b) how deployment is automated; (c) which customer group sees a canary first?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Product Management and the Business Owners. (b) The teams, with the System Team's support. (c) Product Management and the business, using toggles the teams built.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Release on Demand: release immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs. Product Management and Business Owners decide timing. Decoupled release elements. Toggles, canary and progressive rollout. Release governance and automated audit trails. Market rhythms inform timing.
blocks.title: Details to know
