lessons.title: 6.2 · Stabilize
lessons.summary: Keeping the released solution available, secure and recoverable: failover, recovery tests, scaling and security monitoring.

blocks.text:
Stabilize keeps the released solution working well: available, secure and recoverable, so users actually get its value. It is not a hardening phase for unfinished testing, and it is not a code freeze or a slower release cadence.

Stability is designed in. Architecting for operations, with redundancy, telemetry and safe deployment, makes the solution easier to keep stable and to recover.
blocks.title: What stabilize does

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge; not checked against a public SAFe page.
rows: Service continues when a part fails
Confidence that recovery works when needed
Response times held when demand jumps
Threats and vulnerabilities found after release
Solutions that are easy to run and recover
Availability and latency within agreed levels
blocks.title: Stabilize practices

blocks.text: A region fails at a health provider, and traffic moves to a second region without users noticing. Redundancy with automatic failover kept the service up. A weekly backup alone would have helped recovery, but users would have seen an outage.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Stabilize belongs to Release on Demand; monitor and respond belong to Continuous Deployment.

Stabilize does not mean freezing code or releasing less often.

An untested recovery plan is a hope; practise recovery to find the gaps.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Traffic to a new feature is ten times the forecast. Which stabilize practice helps most? Automatic scaling of capacity to match demand.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Threats change after release, so stabilize monitors and patches continuously rather than relying on a one-off penetration test. When an urgent security patch is needed, the fast, trusted pipeline lets it go through the usual tests and controls; manual changes cause drift, and waiting leaves the risk open.

Availability and similar reliability measures, compared with service level objectives, show whether stabilize is working. Feature counts and team size do not.
blocks.title: Security and change after release

blocks.text: A firm's disaster recovery plan says restore in four hours. The first rehearsal takes eleven: a backup is incomplete and two people have left. After three quarterly rehearsals, recovery takes ninety minutes. The plan was not wrong on paper; it was untested.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Pick the practice: (a) one server fails and the service stays up; (b) a new vulnerability is reported in a library you use; (c) find out whether backups really restore.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Redundancy with automatic failover. (b) Continuous security monitoring and a patch through the normal pipeline. (c) A disaster recovery test.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Stabilize: keep the solution available, secure and recoverable after release. Failover and disaster recovery, tested regularly. Automatic scaling. Continuous security monitoring. Architecting for operations. Availability against SLOs. Not hardening, not a freeze.

lessons.title: 6.3 · Measure
lessons.summary: Checking released features against their benefit hypotheses: baselines, A/B tests, segments and lagging outcomes.

blocks.text:
Measure asks whether the released functionality produced the benefit that was predicted in exploration. Passing acceptance tests shows the feature was built as specified. It does not show the feature was worth building.

Learn turns the evidence into a decision to persevere, pivot or stop, and into improvements to the pipeline. What is learned feeds back into Continuous Exploration, which makes the pipeline a loop.
blocks.title: Closing the loop

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of innovation accounting.
rows: Share of customers using the new page twice
blocks.title: Measures and when they arrive

blocks.text: A feature's hypothesis expected 10% more returning customers. The measure activity compares repeat order rates before and after the release, against a baseline from the same season last year. Tests written, commits made and deployment time describe the work, not the result, so they are left out.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
On time and on budget describe delivery; success means the benefit hypothesis was met.

Passing acceptance tests shows the feature was built as specified, not that it was worth building.

Measures chosen after the release tend to flatter the result; agree them up front and build the telemetry to collect them.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Two versions of a sign-up page are shown to random halves of users. What is this? A/B testing.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text:
Segment results before averaging them. A feature used heavily in one region and not at all in another holds two lessons; an average hides both. Compare with a baseline, and where possible with a control group, so seasonal or market effects are not mistaken for the feature's effect.

Targeted toggles let a team collect measures from a chosen group before everyone sees a change. Measured results then feed Continuous Exploration: they confirm or reject hypotheses and suggest new ones.
blocks.title: Reading the results honestly

blocks.text: A team reports success: its feature shipped on time and on budget. Six weeks later, usage telemetry shows almost nobody has found it. The measure activity turns a delivery report into a finding: the feature's entry point is hidden, which becomes the next hypothesis.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: A feature aimed to cut support calls by a fifth. Name one leading indicator and one lagging outcome.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Leading: weekly use of the new self-help page, or the share of users who finish the self-help flow. Lagging: support call volume per thousand customers, compared over several months with a baseline.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Measure: compare results with the benefit hypothesis. Leading indicators and lagging outcomes; baselines; A/B tests; segments; targeted toggles. Measures agreed before release. Results feed Continuous Exploration. Innovation accounting.

lessons.title: 6.4 · Learn
lessons.summary: Pivot, persevere or stop, improving the pipeline itself, and feeding Inspect and Adapt.

blocks.text:
Learn uses the measured results to decide the feature's future, persevere, pivot or stop, and applies lessons to the pipeline itself. What is learned feeds back into Continuous Exploration, which makes the pipeline a loop rather than a line.

A disproved hypothesis is useful evidence: it tells the train where not to invest and frees capacity for better bets. Blame and hiding stop people sharing evidence.
blocks.title: What learn does

rows: Follow-on features into the ART backlog
Partly met; a clear reason why
blocks.title: Decisions after measuring

blocks.text: A loyalty feature had no effect on repeat purchases. Product Management pivots toward a simpler reward, records the learning, and the next exploration cycle starts from a sharper hypothesis. Nobody looks for a team to blame; the evidence was what the release was for.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
Keep building until it works is not learning; it ignores the evidence.

Learn looks at the pipeline as well as the feature: each release shows where the pipeline is slow or fragile.

Inspect and Adapt still runs each PI; release learning feeds it rather than replacing it.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Where does a train turn the PI's issues into improvement backlog items? The problem-solving workshop at Inspect and Adapt.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: After several releases, patterns appear: the same manual approval delays each one, or the same environment fails. Learning turns each repeated delay into an improvement item, such as automating or decentralising the approval, rather than working around it. Teams can map the value stream of the pipeline itself, as in lesson 2, and use the DevOps health radar to choose which activity to improve next.
blocks.title: Improving the pipeline relentlessly

blocks.text: After three releases, a train sees the same manual sign-off delay each one by four days. The retrospective item "chase the approver earlier" changes nothing. At Inspect and Adapt, the problem-solving workshop traces the cause to a policy that treats every change as high risk, and the improvement item automates checks for low-risk changes.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Decide for each: (a) the hypothesis was met and customers ask for more; (b) usage is high but revenue is flat; (c) nobody uses the feature after two months of promotion.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Persevere, with follow-on features in the backlog. (b) Pivot: refine the hypothesis about turning usage into revenue and test it. (c) Stop, and redirect the capacity.
blocks.title: Worked solution

lessons.title: Exam technique
lessons.summary: Pacing for 45 questions in 90 minutes, and the patterns behind the right answers.

blocks.text:
45 questions in 90 minutes is two minutes each. The pass mark of 73% means 33 correct answers, so twelve misses is the limit. Do a first pass answering everything you know, flag the rest, and come back. Unanswered questions count as wrong, so never leave a blank.

Many questions are short scenarios. Read the last sentence first to see what is asked, then read the scenario for the one detail that decides it, such as which activity, which role, or which measure.

lessons.summary: The night-before list for the six domains.

blocks.text: DevOps: mindset, culture and technical practices; deliver value whenever there is a business need; not a team or tool. CALMR: culture, automation, Lean flow, measurement, recovery. Four aspects, sixteen activities; each ART owns its pipeline; continuous security. Value stream maps: process time, lead time, percent complete and accurate; flow efficiency; rolled accuracy; six flow metrics; target the biggest wait; improvement backlog of enablers.
blocks.title: DevOps and value streams

blocks.text: Hypothesize: benefit hypothesis, leading and lagging measures agreed up front, MVP, persevere, pivot or stop. Research: customers, Business Owners, architects, operations; primary and secondary; gemba, personas, journey maps. Architect: releasability, testability, operability, security; runway; four enabler types; NFRs early. Synthesize: vision, roadmap, features with hypotheses and criteria; WSJF = cost of delay / job size; Product Management owns the ART backlog.
blocks.title: Exploration

blocks.text: Develop: stories, TDD and BDD, version control, daily commits, toggles. Build: trunk-based, gated commits, fast builds, build once deploy many, scanning. Test end-to-end: automation, pyramid, test data, service virtualisation, NFRs. Stage: production-like from code, System Demo. Deploy: automation, toggles, dark launch, blue-green, safe schema changes. Verify: in production, smoke tests, key journeys. Monitor: full-stack telemetry, SLOs, alerts on user impact. Respond: restore first, rollback or fix forward, MTTR, blameless reviews.
blocks.title: Integration and deployment

blocks.text: Release when the business needs it; Product Management and Business Owners decide; decoupled release elements; progressive rollout; automated audit trails. Stabilize: failover, tested recovery, scaling, security monitoring; not hardening. Measure: results against the hypothesis; baselines, A/B tests, segments. Learn: persevere, pivot or stop; improve the pipeline; feed exploration and Inspect and Adapt.
blocks.title: Release on Demand

blocks.text: Two minutes a question; twelve misses is the limit. Small batches, shared ownership, hypotheses with measures, quality and security built in, restore first, release on business need.
blocks.title: On the day

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe DevOps?

options.text: A toolchain that replaces manual release approvals
A phase that follows development and testing
A mindset, culture and set of technical practices
A team that owns deployments for the whole train

questions.explanation: SAFe defines DevOps as a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support integration, automation and collaboration. Treating it as a separate team recreates the handoff between builders and operators that DevOps exists to remove. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Source: SAFe · DevOps; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: What does the R in CALMR stand for?

options.text: Recovery
Release
Resilience
Reporting

questions.explanation: CALMR is culture, automation, lean flow, measurement and recovery. Release is tempting because the pipeline ends with Release on Demand, but the mindset names the ability to recover from failure. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe use recovery where the older CALMS model had sharing?

options.text: Sharing applies to operations and leaves out developers
Sharing was replaced by measurement of flow
Sharing is treated as a natural part of culture
Sharing slows teams that work in small batches

questions.explanation: The CALMR article explains that sharing already belongs to culture, so the fifth element is given to recovery. Sharing is still expected; it has moved, it has not been dropped. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: At Norrland Rail, developers are rewarded for shipping features and operations staff are rewarded for uptime, and each group blames the other after a failed release. Which problem does DevOps address here?

options.text: The gap between those who build and those who run the solution
The absence of a single manager for both departments
The shortage of specialist testers inside the operations group
The missing sign-off stage before each production release

questions.explanation: SAFe says DevOps bridges the gap between the people who build solutions and the people who support and maintain them. Adding a sign-off stage widens the gap, because it adds another handoff and delay. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Source: SAFe · DevOps.

questions.prompt: A train at Halden Insurance has automated its builds and deployments, yet failed releases still lead to a search for the person at fault. Which CALMR element needs the most attention?

options.text: Lean flow
Culture
Measurement
Automation

questions.explanation: A culture of shared responsibility treats failure as something the system produced and the group learns from. Automation is already in place here, so more tooling would leave the blame habit untouched. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: A team at Brightwater Bank works on fourteen features at once and finishes few of them. Which CALMR element speaks most directly to this?

options.text: Culture
Lean flow
Measurement
Recovery

questions.explanation: Lean flow covers limiting work in process, reducing batch size and managing queue lengths. Measurement would show the problem, but the remedy is to limit how much is started. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Corvane Logistics want proof that their DevOps investment is working. Which outcome would the CALMR approach point to?

options.text: A shorter mean time to recover after incidents
A higher share of staff holding tool certificates
A longer stabilisation period before each release
A larger number of approval steps completed per release

questions.explanation: Improved mean time to recover is one of the outcomes the CALMR article lists, with faster time to market and fewer defects. More approval steps measure activity in the process, and they slow delivery. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: What does continuous security mean in SAFe DevOps?

options.text: Security testing moves to a hardening iteration
Security work is built into each stage of the pipeline
Security staff review the solution once before release
Security is the duty of the operations group alone

questions.explanation: Continuous security, often called DevSecOps, places security practices such as threat modelling and automated scanning throughout the pipeline. A single review before release finds problems when they are most expensive to fix. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train at Meridian Health runs most checks by hand in the last week of each planning interval. Which step fits continuous testing?

options.text: Reduce testing to the features marked as high risk
Automate tests and run them as each change is integrated
Add a second manual test cycle after the release
Move all testing to a separate quality department before release

questions.explanation: Agile testing in SAFe builds quality in with tests that are automated wherever possible and run continuously. A second manual cycle adds delay and still finds defects late. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Source: SAFe · Agile Testing.

questions.prompt: Which four aspects make up the Continuous Delivery Pipeline, in order?

options.text: Exploration, development, staging, deployment
Planning, development, testing, release management
Integration, exploration, release on demand, deployment
Exploration, integration, deployment, release on demand

questions.explanation: The pipeline runs from Continuous Exploration through Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment to Release on Demand. The second option uses the right names in the wrong order; deployment comes before release. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

questions.prompt: A product at Aster Mobility has a mobile app that could ship daily and a vehicle unit that ships twice a year. What does SAFe suggest?

options.text: Decouple the parts so each releases at its own cadence
Ship the vehicle unit daily to match the app
Hold the app so both parts ship in the same release
Release both parts at the end of each planning interval

questions.explanation: The pipeline article says continuous can mean different things for different parts, and that decoupling avoids one monolithic release. Holding the app delays value that customers could already use. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

questions.prompt: Who builds and manages the Continuous Delivery Pipeline?

options.text: The System Team on behalf of the business owners
Each Agile team separately for its own stories
The Agile Release Train itself, alone or shared
A central release department outside the trains

questions.explanation: SAFe says each Agile Release Train builds and manages, or shares, a pipeline so it can deliver value independently. A central release department takes that independence away and adds a handoff. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline; SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe, what is the goal of DevOps?

options.text: To remove the operations role from the train
To deploy each commit to the whole customer base at once
To deliver value whenever there is a business need
To reach full automation of the manual tasks

questions.explanation: The DevOps article states the goal as delivering value at any time there is a business need. Deploying each commit to all customers confuses deployment with release, which SAFe keeps separate. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Source: SAFe · DevOps.

questions.prompt: A coach at Tallis Energy lists CALMR as one of the technical practice domains of DevOps. What is wrong with that?

options.text: CALMR is the mindset that guides the practice domains
CALMR applies to portfolios, and practice domains to teams
CALMR is the pipeline, and practice domains are its stages
CALMR is a metric set, and practice domains are roles

questions.explanation: SAFe presents CALMR as the mindset behind DevOps and the practice domains as what enables the pipeline. Calling CALMR the pipeline mixes up the mindset with the four pipeline aspects. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · DevOps Practice Domains; SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: A train at Verity Foods deploys once a quarter and each deployment takes a weekend of manual work. Which reasoning matches the DevOps view?

options.text: Add reviewers so each quarterly deployment is safer
Freeze development earlier to give operations more time
Deploy less often so there are fewer risky weekends
Deploy smaller changes more often so each one carries less risk

questions.explanation: Small, frequent, automated deployments lower the risk and cost of each change and speed up learning. Deploying less often makes each batch bigger, which raises the risk it was meant to reduce. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: After an outage at Lumen Travel, the team restored service in ten minutes because it had rehearsed a rollback. Which CALMR element does this show?

options.text: Automation
Measurement
Lean flow
Recovery

questions.explanation: Recovery is about designing and practising for failure so service returns quickly. Automation may have helped, but the rehearsed ability to restore service is what the scenario describes. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: Match each CALMR element to what it stresses.

options.text: Removing manual steps from the pipeline
Data on flow, quality and value
A separate team that owns releases
Small batches and limits on work in process
Shared responsibility across the value stream
Fast restoration of service after failure

questions.explanation: The five elements are culture, automation, lean flow, measurement and recovery. A separate release team is the opposite of shared responsibility and belongs to none of them. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: Which problem was DevOps created to solve?

options.text: The slow speed of programming languages
The wall between building software and running it
The lack of project managers on most software teams
The cost of buying servers for development teams

questions.explanation: DevOps grew out of the conflict between development, rewarded for change, and operations, rewarded for stability. Bringing them together lets change flow safely to production. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company's developers finish features in weeks, but releases wait months for operations. What does this suggest?

options.text: Operations staff need longer working hours
The company should hire more project managers
The developers need to write code faster
The bottleneck is the handoff to operations

questions.explanation: When finished work waits, the constraint is the handoff, not the coding. DevOps addresses it with shared ownership and automation rather than faster typing or longer hours. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe describe DevOps as a mindset and culture rather than a team or a tool?

options.text: Lasting change needs shared ownership across roles
A DevOps team would have too few members to help
Teams and tools are too expensive for most companies
Tools for DevOps do not yet exist on the market

questions.explanation: A separate DevOps team or a new toolchain leaves the old handoffs in place. Change sticks when everyone in the value stream shares responsibility for value in production. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows that DevOps is improving delivery?

options.text: More people with DevOps in their job title
More tools installed in the delivery toolchain
More deployments approved by the change board
Shorter lead time from idea to production

questions.explanation: DevOps aims to deliver value faster and more reliably, so lead time, with quality and recovery measures, shows progress. Tools and titles show activity. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Developers are measured on features shipped and operations on uptime. What does DevOps change?

options.text: Shared goals so both groups own value in production
A single manager to referee disputes between them
Stricter handoffs so that each side is accountable
Separate goals so each group can focus on its own job

questions.explanation: Conflicting goals set the two groups against each other; shared goals, such as reliable, frequent delivery of value, make them partners. Separate goals and stricter handoffs keep the conflict alive. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe tie DevOps to business agility rather than to IT alone?

options.text: Customers get value only when the whole flow is fast
Business agility requires no technical practices
Business staff must write the deployment scripts
IT departments are not allowed to adopt DevOps alone

questions.explanation: A fast pipeline helps only if exploration, funding, release decisions and support move at the same pace. DevOps is one part of an end-to-end flow of value. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does 'shift left' mean in DevOps?

options.text: Delaying testing until the code is complete and stable
Doing testing, security and ops work earlier
Moving operations staff into a separate team on the left
Shifting work from senior to junior engineers

questions.explanation: Shifting left brings quality, security and operational concerns into the earliest steps, where problems are cheapest to fix. Delaying them is the opposite. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which sign shows that a DevOps culture is taking hold?

options.text: Developers hand releases to operations by email
Each failure is traced to the person who caused it
Developers help run and fix what they build
Operations approves each deployment in a weekly meeting

questions.explanation: Shared ownership of production, including on-call and fixes, is the clearest sign of DevOps culture. Approval meetings, blame and email handoffs are the old pattern. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does DevOps reduce the cost of each release over time?

options.text: Automation and small batches make changes cheap and safe
Each release is tested less so it costs less to make
The licence cost of the tools falls each year
Releases are moved to cheaper offshore operations teams

questions.explanation: Automating build, test and deployment lowers the transaction cost of each change, so small, frequent releases become economic and each carries less risk. Cutting testing or moving work offshore does not lower risk. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice best breaks down the wall between development and operations?

options.text: Shared on-call and joint ownership of production
Detailed handoff documents for each release
A rule that operations may refuse any deployment
Separate ticket queues for each group's work

questions.explanation: When both groups share responsibility for production, including being on call, the wall disappears. Queues, documents and vetoes keep it in place. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a DevOps transformation's main goal for customers?

options.text: Deploying code every hour, regardless of the business need
Replacing all operations staff with automation
Using the newest cloud platform available
Delivering value whenever there is a business need

questions.explanation: SAFe's goal for DevOps is the ability to deliver value whenever the business needs it. Frequency for its own sake, removing staff or chasing platforms are not the goal. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A leader asks for a DevOps 'big bang' rollout across all trains at once. What is the better approach?

options.text: Hire a DevOps team to take over all deployments
Buy one toolchain for every train before any change
Wait until each team is fully trained in DevOps
Start where the map shows the biggest delays

questions.explanation: Mapping the value stream shows where delay and rework are worst, so improvement starts where it pays most and builds evidence. A big-bang tool purchase changes little. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · What DevOps is and why it matters”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In CALMR, what does the A stand for?

options.text: Architecture
Automation
Agility
Alignment

questions.explanation: CALMR is Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement and Recovery. Automation removes manual, error-prone steps from the pipeline. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: A train tracks deployment frequency, lead time and recovery time and reviews them each iteration. Which CALMR element is this?

options.text: Lean flow
Automation
Culture
Measurement

questions.explanation: Measurement means collecting and reviewing data on flow, quality and recovery to guide improvement. The numbers named are classic DevOps measures. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: Why is culture the first element of CALMR?

options.text: Culture matters for operations but not for developers
Culture can be bought along with the DevOps tools
Culture is the cheapest element to put in place
Without shared ownership, tools and practices fade

questions.explanation: Automation and metrics only work when people share responsibility and trust each other; otherwise tools are bypassed and numbers are gamed. Culture cannot be bought with tools. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Teams in a value stream work in large batches with long queues between them. Which CALMR element addresses this?

options.text: Recovery
Lean flow
Measurement
Culture

questions.explanation: Lean flow means small batches, limited WIP and short queues, so work moves smoothly through the pipeline. Culture and recovery address other weaknesses. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: Which practice belongs to the recovery element of CALMR?

options.text: Rolling back or fixing forward after a failure
Limiting work in process across the train
Measuring how long each feature takes to deliver
Sharing responsibility between dev and operations

questions.explanation: Recovery is about designing for low-risk releases and fast restoration: rollback, fix-forward, failover. The other options belong to measurement, culture and Lean flow. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: A train automates deployments but keeps blaming individuals after incidents. Which CALMR element is weakest?

options.text: Culture
Lean flow
Measurement
Automation

questions.explanation: Blame drives people to hide mistakes, which undermines learning and recovery. A blameless culture looks for system causes. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe pair measurement with the other CALMR elements?

options.text: Measurement replaces the need for automation
Data lets leaders rank individual engineers
Data shows whether flow and quality improve
Measurement is required by auditors only

questions.explanation: Without measurement, a team cannot tell whether its culture, automation and flow changes are working. Metrics guide the system, not individual ratings. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which CALMR element does a self-service deployment pipeline mainly support?

options.text: Measurement
Automation
Culture
Recovery

questions.explanation: Self-service deployment replaces manual tickets and handoffs with an automated, repeatable path to production. It also supports culture, but automation is its main contribution. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which older DevOps model did CALMR build on?

options.text: ITIL
COBIT
CALMS
PRINCE2

questions.explanation: CALMS ends in Sharing; SAFe treats sharing as part of culture and adds Recovery. ITIL, COBIT and PRINCE2 are service, governance and project frameworks. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Source: SAFe · CALMR.

questions.prompt: A team scores well on automation but poorly on Lean flow. What is the likely symptom?

options.text: Slow pipelines, but work moves quickly between teams
No automated tests at any level of the system
Frequent blame for incidents, with no measurement
Fast pipelines, but work still waits in long queues

questions.explanation: Automation speeds up steps, but large batches and queues between them still dominate lead time. Lean flow addresses the waiting. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · The CALMR approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which aspect of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline comes after Continuous Integration?

options.text: Continuous Exploration
Continuous Deployment
Continuous Testing
Release on Demand

questions.explanation: The four aspects are Continuous Exploration, Continuous Integration, Continuous Deployment and Release on Demand. Continuous Testing is not one of them; testing runs throughout. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

questions.prompt: Which aspect of the pipeline turns a hypothesis into a prioritised backlog of features?

options.text: Continuous Exploration
Continuous Deployment
Release on Demand
Continuous Integration

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration hypothesizes, researches, architects and synthesizes, producing a vision, a roadmap and prioritised features. Integration, deployment and release come after it. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe describe the pipeline as four aspects rather than four phases?

options.text: Each aspect must finish before the next begins
Phases are not allowed in Agile ways of working
They run at the same time, not one after another
Aspects are handled by four separate teams

questions.explanation: At any time, some features are being explored, others integrated, deployed or released. Treating the aspects as phases would recreate waterfall. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team adds a static security scan to each build and threat modelling to exploration. What is this an example of?

options.text: A security phase at the end of the release
Continuous security across the pipeline
Security handled by operations after go-live
Outsourcing security to an external auditor

questions.explanation: Continuous security builds security work into every aspect of the pipeline, so issues surface early. A gate at the end finds them late and expensively. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the DevOps health radar assess?

options.text: The uptime of each production server in the data centre
The maturity of the pipeline's sixteen activities
The health of each engineer's working hours
The cost of the delivery toolchain per team

questions.explanation: The radar scores each of the sixteen activities, four per pipeline aspect, so a train can see where to improve first. It assesses capability, not people. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which items flow through the Continuous Delivery Pipeline?

options.text: Employees, from hiring to promotion
Budgets, from request to approval
Features, from hypothesis to released value
Servers, from purchase to retirement

questions.explanation: Features enter as hypotheses in exploration and leave as released, measured value. The pipeline is a flow of value, not of assets or people. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why must the pipeline include releasing on demand as well as deploying?

options.text: Customers get value only when it is released
Releasing is a technical step with no business input
Release on demand replaces the need for testing
Deployment alone is enough to satisfy every customer

questions.explanation: Deployed but unreleased functionality creates no value; release on demand lets the business choose when customers receive it, then measure and learn. Testing still runs throughout. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice best embeds security in Continuous Integration?

options.text: Security sign-off by email after deployment
A yearly audit of the source code by hand
Automated security tests on each build
A penetration test once before each major release

questions.explanation: Automated security checks, such as static analysis and dependency scanning, give feedback on every change. Occasional tests and audits find problems late. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train runs Continuous Exploration only once a year in a big planning event. What is the problem?

options.text: It should run all the time, feeding the backlog
Exploration belongs to the portfolio, not to the train
Exploration should run only after each release is done
Exploration needs no input from customers or users

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration keeps hypotheses and features flowing as the market changes. A yearly event freezes the backlog and delays learning. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does continuous security differ from a security gate at the end?

options.text: Security work is in each aspect, so issues surface early
Continuous security applies only to production servers
A gate at the end finds issues earlier than continuous checks
Continuous security removes the need for any security staff

questions.explanation: Spreading security across exploration, integration, deployment and release finds issues when they are cheap to fix. Security specialists remain, working within the flow. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows that the pipeline is a train-level responsibility?

options.text: A central team owns the pipeline for every ART
Each developer runs a private pipeline of their own
The ART builds and improves its own pipeline
The vendor of the tools maintains the pipeline

questions.explanation: In SAFe the ART builds and manages its pipeline, with help from shared services and the System Team. A distant central owner recreates handoffs. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.3 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and continuous security”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of mapping a value stream?

options.text: To document the tools used at each step
To compare the output of individual team members
To see how work flows and where it waits
To record who is accountable for each defect

questions.explanation: A value stream map makes the steps, handoffs and delays visible so the group can decide what to improve. It looks at the system; using it to rate people destroys the trust the exercise needs. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In value stream mapping, what is process time?

options.text: The elapsed time from the request to its delivery
The time someone is actively working on the item in a step
The time an item waits before a step picks it up
The time needed to repair work returned by a later step

questions.prompt: What does percent complete and accurate tell you about a step?

10 percent

180 percent
20 percent

questions.prompt: A map at Calder Freight shows that work spends two days in testing and eleven days waiting for a test environment. Where should the group look first?

questions.prompt: Who should take part in a value stream mapping workshop?

File the current state map as evidence for the next audit

questions.prompt: Which flow metric counts the work items currently in progress?

Flow distribution
Flow velocity

Flow predictability
Flow velocity

questions.prompt: Flow load at Stonebridge Telecom keeps rising while flow velocity stays flat. What is the likely effect?

Outcomes, flow and competency

questions.prompt: A portfolio at Tern Aviation wants to know whether its solutions meet customer needs. Which measurement domain answers that?

Outcomes

questions.prompt: A manager at Ivel Pharma proposes using the value stream map to rank teams by their process time. What is the best response?

questions.prompt: Which idea from Lean thinking does mapping serve most directly?

Identify the value stream, then make value flow

questions.prompt: The DevOps health radar at Kestrel Bank shows low scores for monitoring and for responding. Which pipeline aspect holds both?

questions.prompt: What does a current-state value stream map show?

The ideal process the team hopes to reach next year

questions.explanation: A current-state map shows reality: steps, the waits between them, handoffs and rework. The ideal process belongs on the future-state map. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Where should a value stream map start and end?

questions.prompt: Why should the people who do the work draw the map rather than managers alone?

questions.prompt: During a mapping workshop, the team argues about how the process should work. What should the facilitator do?

Ask the most senior person to describe the process
Skip the disputed steps to save time in the workshop
Map today's process first, then discuss the future

questions.prompt: Which three numbers are usually recorded for each step in a value stream map?

Story points, velocity and the defects found in the step
Cost, headcount and the number of tools used in the step

questions.prompt: A map shows work passing through nine handoffs between five departments. What does this suggest?

options.text: Delay and rework at handoffs; use fewer steps
More approvals are needed to control the handoffs
Each department should write longer handoff documents
The process is working well, since many people check it

questions.prompt: Besides the map itself, what is the main output of a value stream mapping workshop?

A ranking of the slowest people involved
Agreed improvement items with owners
A new organisation chart for the teams

questions.explanation: The map is a means: the workshop should end with a few prioritised improvements that someone owns. Ranking people turns it into blame. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which part of a value stream map shows the wait between two steps?

The percent complete and accurate of each step

The delay time drawn between the process boxes

questions.prompt: A team maps its process and finds that one step is done by a single person with a two-week queue. What has the map revealed?

A bottleneck that constrains the whole flow

questions.explanation: A step with a long queue in front of it limits the throughput of the whole stream. The fix is about capacity and flow, such as cross-training, not about the person. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe recommend mapping from the customer's point of view?

options.text: Value and delay are what customers experience
Internal steps are not part of a value stream
Customers draw the map during the workshop
Customers are required to approve every map

questions.explanation: Starting from the customer keeps the focus on the flow of value, including internal steps, rather than on any one department's efficiency. Internal steps are still mapped. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which scope is best for a first value stream mapping workshop?

options.text: The finance approval process for budgets
One feature's journey from idea to production
The coding step alone, since it is the core
All processes in the whole enterprise at once

questions.explanation: A single, recent, representative flow is concrete enough to map accurately in a workshop and still shows end-to-end delays. Mapping everything at once loses detail. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a future-state value stream map?

options.text: A map that only managers are allowed to see
A copy of the current map with costs added
A forecast of next year's budget for the train
A design of the improved flow to aim for

questions.explanation: The future-state map shows the flow the team aims for, with fewer waits and handoffs, and guides the improvement backlog. It is not a budget or a private document. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Mapping the current value stream”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team maps a process and finds that most lead time is waiting for approvals. Which improvement is likely to help most?

Speed up the coding step with better tools

Add a second approval step for extra safety

Each person sees their part, not the waits between

The company's organisation chart and job titles

The time between two planning intervals

60 percent
54 percent

questions.prompt: Why can improving one step's process time do little for the whole value stream?

Lead time depends on the number of steps alone

Flow time

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether its value stream improvements worked. Which measure fits best?

questions.prompt: Why can adding more people to a slow step fail to shorten lead time?

questions.prompt: Which improvement addresses a low percent complete and accurate at a requirements step?

questions.prompt: What does Continuous Exploration produce for the train?

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Continuous Exploration?

questions.prompt: A product manager at Ardent Payments treats a customer request as a confirmed requirement and schedules it. How does Continuous Exploration view the request?

questions.prompt: What is a benefit hypothesis?

questions.prompt: What is a Minimum Viable Product in SAFe?

The smallest release that customers will pay for

questions.explanation: SAFe defines the MVP as an early and minimal version of a solution used to prove or disprove the epic hypothesis. The smallest sellable release is closer to a minimum marketable feature, which serves a different purpose. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: The MVP for an epic at Solace Health shows that clinics do not use the new booking flow. What should happen?

options.text: Increase the budget so adoption can catch up
Pivot or stop, since the hypothesis was not supported
Hide the result until the next portfolio review
Complete the remaining features as planned

questions.explanation: Lean startup thinking uses the MVP result to decide whether to persevere, pivot or stop. Finishing the plan regardless is the sunk-cost response the hypothesis-driven approach is meant to prevent. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure would serve as a leading indicator for a hypothesis that a new checkout raises annual revenue at Juniper Outdoor?

options.text: The number of stories completed for the checkout
The team's velocity across the planning interval
The share of baskets that reach payment this week
The annual revenue reported next year

questions.explanation: A leading indicator is an early, measurable signal that predicts the business outcome. Annual revenue is the lagging result, and completed stories measure output with no link to customer behaviour. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is innovation accounting used for?

options.text: Recording hours spent on the IP iteration
Allocating the innovation budget across trains
Judging a hypothesis with early, actionable measures
Capitalising the cost of software development

questions.explanation: Innovation accounting uses leading indicators to evaluate a hypothesis long before financial results arrive. It sounds like a finance practice, but it is a learning tool from Lean startup. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who should Product Management involve during exploration?

options.text: Customers, business owners, architects and Agile teams
The portfolio office and no one from the teams
The marketing group, after features are defined
The operations group, once deployment begins

questions.explanation: The exploration article names customers, suppliers, partners, business owners, Agile teams and others as stakeholders. Leaving the teams out until features are defined loses their knowledge of what is feasible. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Wren Logistics wants to learn how dispatchers work. Which approach gives primary research?

options.text: Compare the feature lists of two competitors
Read an analyst report on the logistics market
Review last year's support ticket categories
Spend a day watching them at their desks

questions.explanation: Primary research gathers first-hand evidence, for example by observing users where they work. Analyst reports and competitor comparisons are secondary research, useful but one step removed. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does Lean UX emphasise?

options.text: Pixel-level sign-off by stakeholders
A separate design phase for each feature
Complete design before development
Iterative learning and customer outcomes

questions.explanation: SAFe describes Lean UX as a team-based approach that focuses on iterative learning, overall experience and customer outcomes over a theoretically ideal design. Designing everything first delays the feedback it relies on. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Source: SAFe · Lean UX.

questions.prompt: A train at Greyfell Bank wants to deploy daily but its services share one database schema that needs a coordinated change for each feature. Which exploration activity addresses this?

options.text: Collaborate and research
Architect
Hypothesize
Synthesize

questions.explanation: The architect activity shapes the solution for continuous delivery, including the runway that lets features flow with little redesign. Synthesize turns the ideas into backlog features and comes after this thinking. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Architectural Runway.

questions.prompt: What is the Architectural Runway?

options.text: A long-range plan for replacing the legacy systems across the portfolio
Existing code, components and infrastructure for near-term features
The list of approved technology standards
A reserved iteration for architecture work

questions.explanation: The runway is the existing code, components and technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features with minimal redesign and delay. It is something that exists, not a plan or a standards list. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Architectural Runway; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A train at Petrel Media relies on emergent design alone across twelve teams. Which problem does SAFe expect?

options.text: Slower teams because of central approval
Too much documentation of design decisions
One-off solutions that are hard to change and reuse
Features that are too small to demonstrate

questions.explanation: The runway article says that at scale, emergent design alone leads to missing standards, one-off solutions and poor interoperability. Central approval is a risk of the opposite extreme, heavy up-front design. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Architectural Runway.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe balance design at scale?

options.text: It replaces emergent design with a central blueprint
It leaves all design to each team's judgement
It combines emergent design with intentional architecture
It fixes the architecture before the first interval

questions.explanation: SAFe pairs emergent design with intentional architecture, which adds planning and coordination across teams. Replacing emergence with a blueprint returns to big design up front. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Architectural Runway.

questions.prompt: What is an enabler?

options.text: A feature requested by an internal customer
A team member who removes impediments for the train during an interval
A tool that automates part of the pipeline
A backlog item that extends the runway or improves the value stream

questions.explanation: Enablers are backlog items that extend the Architectural Runway or improve the performance of the development value stream. They are work items, so they are estimated, prioritised and demonstrated like any other. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Enablers; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A train at Marlow Energy needs a new automated test environment. Which type of enabler is this?

options.text: Compliance
Architecture
Infrastructure
Exploration

questions.explanation: Infrastructure enablers create and improve development and runtime environments. Architecture enablers build the runway in the solution itself, which is close but concerns components and design. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Enablers.

questions.prompt: A team at Sable Insurance must automate evidence for a regulatory audit. Which enabler type fits?

options.text: Compliance
Infrastructure
Exploration
Architecture

questions.explanation: Compliance enablers cover verification and validation, audits and approvals, and policy automation. Infrastructure is tempting because automation is involved, but the purpose here is meeting a regulation. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Enablers.

questions.prompt: What are nonfunctional requirements?

options.text: Requirements that were rejected by the business as too costly
System qualities that guide design and act as constraints
Features that have no visible user interface
Tasks that support a story but add no value

questions.explanation: NFRs are system qualities such as security, performance and scalability that guide the design and often constrain the backlogs. They are not a kind of feature without a screen. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Nonfunctional Requirements; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A team at Hollin Rail adds a performance requirement to a single story and forgets it afterwards. Why is that a weak way to handle an NFR?

options.text: An NFR is tested once by the System Team, at the end of the planning interval
An NFR belongs to the architect and not to teams
An NFR must be written as a separate feature
An NFR constrains many items and is checked again in each increment

questions.explanation: NFRs act as constraints across backlogs and are revisited as part of the definition of done for each iteration, interval or release. Treating one as a single story lets later work break it unnoticed. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Nonfunctional Requirements.

questions.prompt: During exploration at Tarn Systems, an architect insists on feature toggles and backward-compatible interfaces. What is the architect designing for?

options.text: Compliance, so audits take less effort
Usability, so customers need less training
Releasability, so deployment and release can be separated
Capacity, so several teams can work on one component in parallel

questions.explanation: Toggles and compatible interfaces let code reach production without changing behaviour until the business chooses to release. This is a design decision, which is why it starts in exploration and not at deployment time. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A security specialist at Elmfield Bank joins exploration to identify how a new payment feature could be attacked. Which practice is this?

options.text: Penetration testing
Threat modelling
Chaos engineering
Static code analysis

questions.explanation: Threat modelling examines a design for possible attacks before code is written, which is why it sits in the architect activity. Penetration testing needs a running system and happens later. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a feature is correct in SAFe?

options.text: It needs portfolio approval and a Lean business case before work starts
It is a technical task that supports a story
It delivers business value and fits within one planning interval
It fits within one iteration for a single team

questions.explanation: A feature is solution functionality that delivers business value, meets a stakeholder need and is sized for one train in one planning interval. The portfolio approval and Lean business case belong to epics. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Exploration at Dunmore Travel has produced validated ideas. What does the synthesize activity do with them?

options.text: Deploys them to staging so they appear in the next system demo
Hands them to operations as change requests
Commits them to version control as stories
Shapes them into prioritised features in the ART Backlog

questions.explanation: Synthesize turns the understanding gained into a vision, a roadmap and prioritised features ready for PI Planning. Committing work to version control is the develop activity in Continuous Integration. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: How is Weighted Shortest Job First calculated?

options.text: Job size divided by cost of delay
Business value multiplied by job size
Cost of delay divided by job size
Cost of delay added to job size

questions.explanation: WSJF divides the cost of delay by the job size, so valuable, short jobs come first. Inverting the fraction would favour the largest and least urgent work. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: Which three parts make up the cost of delay in WSJF?

options.text: User-business value, time criticality, risk reduction or opportunity enablement
Development cost, testing cost and the operating cost over the first three years
Revenue, market share, customer satisfaction
Story points, team capacity, iteration length

questions.explanation: Cost of delay adds user and business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. Development and testing costs relate to the job size, which is the denominator. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Two backlog items at Corran Health have the same cost of delay. Item A is a 3 in size and item B is an 8. Which goes first under WSJF?

options.text: Item B, since the larger job delivers more value
Neither, since equal cost of delay means a tie
Item B, since large items should start early
Item A, since the smaller job gives a higher score

questions.explanation: With equal cost of delay, the smaller job has the higher WSJF score and delivers its value sooner. Starting the larger job first delays both. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: A pipeline automation enabler at Lyle Telecom has a higher WSJF score than a customer feature. A stakeholder says customer features come first. What does SAFe economics say?

options.text: Sequence by WSJF, since the enabler has the better return
Sequence the enabler last, since it has no user value
Sequence the feature first, since enablers are overhead
Split capacity evenly, whatever the scores say

questions.explanation: WSJF applies to the whole backlog, and an enabler that removes delay from each later feature can carry a high cost of delay. Treating enablers as overhead leaves the pipeline slow and makes every feature more expensive. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Varley Foods writes a full requirements document for the year before any team sees it. Which exploration idea does this conflict with?

options.text: A vision that stays stable for the year
A roadmap that shows committed dates for the next four quarters
A fixed scope agreed with business owners
A steady flow of small features that give fast feedback

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration replaces large up-front requirements with a continuous flow of features that are split into small stories. A year of fixed requirements delays feedback until it is expensive to act on. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: Match each enabler type to its work.

options.text: Verification, audits and policy automation
Building the Architectural Runway
Research and prototyping to understand options
Marketing a released feature
Improving development and runtime environments

questions.explanation: The four enabler types are exploration, architecture, infrastructure and compliance. Marketing a feature is a release activity and not an enabler type. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Enablers.

questions.prompt: Put the four activities of Continuous Exploration in order.

options.text: Collaborate and research
Hypothesize
Architect
Synthesize

questions.explanation: Exploration starts with a hypothesis, tests it through collaboration and research, shapes the architecture and then synthesizes the result into features. Synthesize comes last because it needs the outputs of the other three. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: SDP (6.0).

questions.prompt: What is the first activity of Continuous Exploration?

options.text: Collaborate and research
Synthesize
Hypothesize
Architect

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration runs hypothesize, collaborate and research, architect, and synthesize. Ideas start as hypotheses to be tested, not as requirements. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a well-formed hypothesis for a new feature?

options.text: Faster checkout is the top request from sales
We believe faster checkout lifts orders by 5%
Customers have always wanted a faster checkout
We will build a faster checkout in the next PI

questions.explanation: A hypothesis states a belief and the measurable result that would confirm it. A plan, a sales request or a claim about the past cannot be tested. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe treat new ideas as hypotheses rather than requirements?

options.text: So they can be written faster than requirements
So they are tested with evidence before full investment
So that teams can ignore them if they are too difficult
So product managers do not need to talk to customers

questions.explanation: Treating ideas as hypotheses means building the smallest test, measuring the result and deciding to pivot, persevere or stop. Requirements assume the answer is already known. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a leading indicator in Continuous Exploration?

options.text: A final business result reported at year end
A metric chosen by the team leader of the train
A count of the features delivered in the PI
An early measure that predicts the end result

questions.explanation: Leading indicators move early, during an MVP or soon after release, and point toward the business outcome. They let the train decide before the lagging result arrives. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure is the best leading indicator for a feature meant to cut support calls?

options.text: Weekly use of the new self-help page
Annual customer satisfaction survey results
The number of developers who built the feature
Total revenue at the end of the financial year

questions.explanation: Self-help usage moves within days and predicts fewer calls. Annual surveys and revenue arrive too late to steer the feature. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team wants to test whether customers would pay for a premium tier before building it. Which approach fits?

options.text: Ask the sales team whether they think it would sell
Build the full tier and launch it to all customers
Copy a competitor's premium tier exactly
Offer it on a landing page and measure sign-ups

questions.explanation: A landing page or similar experiment tests demand cheaply before anything is built. Opinions and copies do not test this market. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of skipping the hypothesize activity?

options.text: Building unneeded features, found only after release
Release on demand will no longer be possible at all
Architects will not be able to design the runway
Developers will have too little work to do in the PI

questions.explanation: Without a hypothesis and measures, nobody knows whether a feature is valuable until it has been built and released, when changing course is most expensive. Hypotheses make the expected value explicit up front. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In the Lean Startup terms SAFe uses, what does an MVP test?

options.text: The full solution's performance under peak load
The riskiest assumptions of an idea, cheaply
The team's ability to deliver on a fixed date
The vendor's support for the chosen platform

questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest thing that can test whether the idea's key assumptions hold. Load testing and vendor support are later concerns. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: MVP results are mixed: usage is high but revenue is flat. What should the team do?

options.text: Ignore the data and go on to build the full scope
Stop the work immediately, since revenue is still flat
Refine the hypothesis and run a further experiment
Declare success at once, since usage is already high

questions.explanation: Mixed evidence calls for learning: a sharper hypothesis about why usage does not turn into revenue, tested cheaply. Declaring success or stopping both ignore half the data. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who should define the success measures for a hypothesis?

options.text: The developers, after the feature has been built
The finance team, at the end of the financial year
Product Management and the business, up front
The vendor, based on its other customers' results

questions.explanation: Measures set in advance by those who own the outcome keep the test honest. Measures chosen afterwards tend to be the ones that look good. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a hypothesis name both a leading indicator and a business outcome?

options.text: The indicator is for engineers; the outcome is for finance
Two measures double the chance of reporting success
The outcome is reached first and the indicator follows
The indicator steers early; the outcome confirms the value

questions.explanation: Leading indicators support fast pivot-or-persevere decisions, and the outcome confirms whether the value really arrived. Each alone is incomplete. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which source of ideas belongs in the hypothesize activity?

options.text: Only the requests of the most senior stakeholder
Ideas from last year's plan, used unchanged
Customer feedback, market data and team insights
Features copied directly from the main competitor

questions.explanation: Good hypotheses come from many sources, including customers, data, the market and the people who build and support the solution. A single senior voice narrows the options. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a Minimum Marketable Feature?

options.text: The cheapest feature that marketing can promote
The smallest feature that delivers real value
A feature defined in full detail before any work
A prototype that is never shown to customers

questions.explanation: An MMF is the least functionality that provides real value and can be released, which gets feedback and returns sooner. It is not a prototype or a marketing item. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An experiment shows that nobody uses a new feature. What is the most valuable outcome?

options.text: Hiding the result to protect the team's morale
Building the rest of the feature to improve usage
Repeating the same experiment until it succeeds
Stopping early, before more money is spent on it

questions.explanation: A disproved hypothesis is useful: it frees capacity for better ideas. Building more or hiding the result wastes the learning. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does hypothesis-driven development change what 'done' means for a feature?

options.text: Done means the feature has been demonstrated once
Done includes measuring whether the value arrived
Done means marketing has announced the feature
Done means the code is merged and the tests pass

questions.explanation: Under hypothesis-driven development, the feature's job is the benefit, so it is not finished until the measures show whether the benefit arrived. Merged code is only a step. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A Business Owner insists a feature is certain to succeed and needs no measures. How should Product Management respond?

options.text: Refuse to build the feature until it is shown to work
Measure only the cost of building the feature
Accept, since the Business Owner knows the market
Agree measures anyway, so the result can be shown

questions.explanation: Even confident bets benefit from measures: they prove the value and catch surprises early. Refusing to build would block a possibly good idea. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which Lean Startup cycle does SAFe use to describe learning from experiments?

options.text: Plan, do, check
Design, test, release
Build, measure, learn
Code, deploy, monitor

questions.explanation: Build, measure, learn turns ideas into experiments and results into decisions. Plan, Do, Check, Adjust is SAFe's cycle for fast integrated learning in development. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which hypothesis is easiest to test quickly?

options.text: A company-wide reorganisation judged annually
A complete platform rebuild judged after two years
A brand campaign judged by awareness surveys
A small change measured with real users in weeks

questions.explanation: Small changes with short feedback loops give evidence fast and cheaply. Large initiatives judged after years give little chance to adjust. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Hypothesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the collaborate and research activity aim to do?

options.text: Write out the detailed design for each feature
Approve the train's budget for the next PI
Understand customer needs and the wider context
Test the deployed solution in the live environment

questions.explanation: Collaborate and research brings customers, Product Management, Business Owners, architects and others together to understand needs and context. Design and testing come later in the pipeline. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: Which research method gives the richest view of how users really work?

options.text: Asking the account managers
Sending a short online survey
Observing them at their place of work
Reading the support ticket counts

questions.explanation: Observation, the gemba, reveals workarounds and context that users rarely mention in surveys. Second-hand sources miss them. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between primary and secondary market research?

options.text: Primary is done by managers; secondary by the teams
Primary is first-hand; secondary uses existing data
Primary is qualitative; secondary is always numerical
Primary is about prices; secondary is about features

questions.explanation: Primary research collects new data directly, such as interviews and observation; secondary research uses existing sources, such as market reports. Both can be qualitative or quantitative. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which tool summarises a type of user's goals, behaviours and pain points?

options.text: A persona
A value stream map
A RACI matrix
A burn-down chart

questions.explanation: A persona is a realistic, fictional user built from research, which keeps real needs in view during design. The other tools track work, flow and responsibilities. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which tool shows the steps a buyer goes through, with their feelings at each step?

options.text: A user story map
A customer journey map
A team Kanban board
A detailed persona

questions.explanation: A journey map follows the customer's experience step by step, with emotions and pain points, showing where to improve. A persona describes the user rather than the journey. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should architects join exploration instead of waiting for finished features?

options.text: Architects are the main source of customer insight
Research cannot start without an architecture diagram
Technical options shape what can be built and run
Architects must approve every feature before research

questions.explanation: Architects help judge feasibility and spot enablers early, so features are shaped by what can be built and run. Waiting creates rework. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who brings the voice of operations into exploration?

options.text: The marketing team, from its campaign data
The finance team, from its cost reports
The sales team, from its quota results
The people who run and support it

questions.explanation: Operations and support know how the solution behaves in production and what users struggle with. Including them early is part of DevOps. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does a gemba walk involve?

options.text: A walk-through of the release notes with sales
Going to where the work happens to observe it
A team-building walk at the start of a PI
Walking through the code in a review session

questions.explanation: Gemba is the Lean term for the place where value is created; walking it means observing the real work. It replaces assumptions with first-hand facts. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A product manager has strong opinions about what customers want but no data. What should come first?

options.text: Build the most popular idea and see what happens
Ask the team to vote on which opinions are right
Talk to and observe users to test those opinions
Write requirements based on the opinions to save time

questions.explanation: Opinions are hypotheses; research tests them cheaply before money is spent on building. Votes and guesses do not add evidence. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is customer research continuous rather than a one-off phase?

options.text: A one-off phase is forbidden by SAFe
Research teams need work between projects
Customers expect to be contacted every week
Needs and markets change, so insight ages

questions.explanation: What customers need shifts with competitors, technology and their own situations, so research runs alongside delivery, feeding the backlog. A one-off study goes stale within months. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which collaborator is most important when exploring a feature that changes billing rules?

options.text: A designer who knows the brand's colour scheme
The facilities team that manages the office
Finance specialists who know that domain well
An external vendor selling a billing product

questions.explanation: Subject-matter experts for the domain being changed hold the rules, exceptions and risks the feature must handle. Brand and facilities are not relevant here. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which design thinking tool helps a team understand what a user says, thinks, does and feels?

options.text: A risk register
An empathy map
A WSJF table
A story map
