questions.explanation: Empathy maps capture what a user says, thinks, does and feels, building shared understanding of their view. A story map organises stories along the user's journey. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which input best tells a train how a released feature is actually used?

options.text: Telemetry from production
The date it was planned in PI Planning
The number of story points it took to build
The opinion of the developer who built it

questions.explanation: Production telemetry shows real usage, which feeds the next round of exploration. Effort and opinions do not describe use. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why involve Business Owners in exploration?

options.text: They write the code for the highest-value features
They hold the context and decide what is valuable
They set the team's iteration goals each week
They must test each feature before it is released

questions.explanation: Business Owners bring strategy, market knowledge and accountability for value, which shapes hypotheses and priorities. They do not code, test or set team goals. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Research shows two user groups need different things from one feature. What should exploration produce?

options.text: A feature for the larger group only, ignoring the other
Hypotheses for each group, tested separately
A delay until the two groups agree with each other
One averaged feature that partly suits both groups

questions.explanation: Different needs call for separate hypotheses and measures, so each can be tested and prioritised. An averaged feature often suits neither group. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps a distributed team research customers it cannot visit?

options.text: Waiting until travel is possible again
Reading the competitor's marketing pages
Guessing from the team's own experience
Remote interviews and screen sharing

questions.explanation: Remote interviews and observing users share their screens give first-hand insight without travel. Guessing and waiting give none. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main output of collaborate and research for the next activity?

options.text: A finished design document signed off by the customer
A final budget for the whole solution
A deployed prototype running in production
Insight that shapes the architecture and features

questions.explanation: Research feeds the architect and synthesize activities with what customers need and the context, so the solution and features fit. It does not produce signed designs or budgets. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team surveys only its happiest customers about a new feature. What is the problem?

options.text: Happy customers never answer surveys honestly
The survey should ask about the competitors
Surveys are not allowed in SAFe exploration
The sample is biased, so the results mislead

questions.explanation: Asking only satisfied customers hides the needs of others, including those who might leave. A representative sample gives a truer picture. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Collaborate and research”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In Continuous Exploration, what does the architect activity aim to ensure?

options.text: The architect approves each team's story estimates
Every team uses the same programming language
The architecture is fully documented before any coding
It can be built, tested, released and run easily

questions.explanation: Architecting for continuous delivery means designing for testability, releasability, operability and security from the start. Full up-front documentation is not the goal. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: Which design choice most helps operations run a new service?

options.text: A detailed handbook written after the release
Built-in logs, metrics and traces
A single shared server for all services
A manual restart procedure for each failure

questions.explanation: Telemetry designed in from the start lets operations see and diagnose the service in production. Handbooks and manual procedures react after the fact. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A new feature must be deployed early but hidden until a marketing launch. Which architectural support is needed?

options.text: A code freeze until the launch date
Feature toggles designed into the solution
A separate long-lived branch for the feature
A second copy of the production system

questions.explanation: Toggles let code be deployed and verified in production while staying invisible, so release is a business decision. A long-lived branch delays integration instead. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should NFRs be considered in exploration rather than added before release?

options.text: NFRs belong to the portfolio rather than to trains
They shape architecture, which is costly to change
NFRs change too often to be written down early
NFRs are only tested by operations after release

questions.explanation: Performance, security and reliability needs drive architectural choices, so learning them late forces costly redesign. They are tested throughout the pipeline. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which architectural enabler would most reduce the risk of each deployment?

options.text: A larger change board to review each deployment
A rule to deploy only on the first Monday of the month
Automated blue-green or canary deployment support
A longer test phase before each release window

questions.explanation: Blue-green and canary deployments limit exposure and make rollback quick, reducing risk on every deployment. More reviews and rarer deployments make each one riskier. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does architectural runway allow a train to do?

options.text: Avoid writing tests for the next few features
Skip PI Planning for the next two PIs
Build upcoming features without redesign
Release features without any business input

questions.explanation: Runway is the existing technical foundation that upcoming features need, so they can be built without first redesigning the system. Enablers extend it. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Architectural Runway.

questions.prompt: A train's runway is nearly used up. What should exploration plan?

options.text: A pause in all work until a new design is done
Enablers that extend the runway ahead of time
A switch to a new technology for every service
More features, so the runway is used up faster

questions.explanation: Architectural and infrastructure enablers extend the runway before the features that need it. Pausing all work or switching everything is out of proportion. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should architects consider releasability in exploration?

options.text: So deploy and release separate without later rework
So that releases can be made without any testing
So that marketing can choose the colour of new features
So the architects can approve each release in person

questions.explanation: Separating deployment from release needs design support, such as toggles and backward-compatible changes. Adding it late means rework. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which input from operations is most useful to the architect activity?

options.text: The marketing plan for the next product launch
The holiday calendar of the operations team
The list of features sales wants next quarter
Incident, capacity and performance data

questions.explanation: Production data shows where the current architecture strains, which guides design and enablers. Marketing and sales lists inform other activities. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A feature needs a data store that no team has used before. Which enabler type fits a short investigation first?

options.text: Architectural enabler
Exploration enabler
Infrastructure enabler
Compliance enabler

questions.explanation: Exploration enablers, such as spikes and prototypes, build the knowledge needed to choose and design. Architectural enablers then build the chosen foundation. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Source: SAFe · Enablers.

questions.prompt: Why should the architect activity consider operability as well as functionality?

options.text: Functionality is designed by the operations team
An unreliable solution gives users little value
Operability can be added cheaply after release
Operability is the only quality that customers notice

questions.explanation: Users get value only from a solution that runs reliably and can be supported; designing for operations from the start is part of DevOps. Retrofitting it is costly. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice lets a team test an architecture choice with low risk before committing to it?

options.text: A vote among the developers on the train
A time-boxed spike or prototype
A decision by the most senior architect alone
A full rewrite of the existing system

questions.explanation: A short spike or prototype produces evidence about an option cheaply, so the commitment rests on facts. Votes and seniority do not. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Architect”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the synthesize activity produce?

options.text: Deployed code running in the production environment
A signed contract with the chosen technology vendor
A vision, a roadmap and prioritised features
A final test report for the release

questions.explanation: Synthesize turns exploration's results into a vision, a roadmap and a prioritised ART backlog of features ready for PI Planning. Code and tests come later in the pipeline. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: Which artefact shows the planned timing of features over the next few PIs?

options.text: The team backlog
The risk register
The deployment log
The solution roadmap

questions.explanation: A roadmap shows expected deliverables and milestones over a time horizon, giving stakeholders a forecast. Team backlogs hold stories for the near term. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does synthesize end with features ready for PI Planning?

options.text: PI Planning is the only event where features exist
Teams are not allowed to refine features later
Features must be coded before PI Planning starts
PI Planning needs defined, ranked work to plan

questions.explanation: Content readiness for PI Planning means the top features are defined and ranked, so teams can plan them. Teams still refine features further as they work. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which feature description is ready for the ART backlog?

options.text: A list of the developers who will build it
A full specification with screen layouts for each step
A one-word title chosen by the sales director
A name, a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: A feature needs a short name, a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria. A full specification is more than needed, and a title alone is too little. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In WSJF, which number goes in the denominator?

options.text: Time criticality
Cost of delay
Job size
User-business value

questions.explanation: WSJF is cost of delay divided by job size, used as a proxy for duration. Time criticality and user-business value are parts of cost of delay. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: Feature A has a cost of delay of 20 and a size of 5; feature B has a cost of delay of 30 and a size of 10. Which goes first?

options.text: Feature A, with WSJF 4
Feature B, since its cost of delay is higher
Both together, since they are close
Feature B, with WSJF 3

questions.explanation: A scores 20 / 5 = 4 and B scores 30 / 10 = 3, so A goes first despite B's higher cost of delay. Doing both at once raises WIP and delays both. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: Why is the ART backlog managed as a Kanban system?

options.text: It replaces the need for PI Planning
It lets the RTE assign features to individuals
It stores the code for each feature
It shows flow and limits work in each state

questions.explanation: A Kanban system shows features moving through states, with WIP limits that keep exploration in step with delivery capacity. PI Planning still happens. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Product Management has fifty features in the ART backlog for one PI of capacity. What should synthesize do?

options.text: Rank them by WSJF and refine the top ones
Rank them by the order they were requested
Refine all fifty in full detail before ranking
Ask teams to commit to all fifty in the PI

questions.explanation: Ranking first and refining only the top items avoids wasting effort on features that will not be built soon. Committing to all fifty ignores capacity. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does a solution vision describe?

options.text: The future state of the solution and why it matters
The detailed design of each component in the solution
The budget for each team over the next year
The test plan for the next major release

questions.explanation: The vision describes where the solution is heading and the value it will create, guiding features and roadmap. Detailed designs and budgets are other artefacts. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice keeps the ART backlog healthy between PI Planning events?

options.text: Letting each team reorder the backlog alone
Freezing the backlog until the next PI Planning
Regular refinement of features with the teams
Adding every new idea straight to the top

questions.explanation: Continuous refinement keeps the next features understood, sized and ranked, so PI Planning is ready. Freezing or unfiltered additions undermine flow. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should synthesize consider capacity allocation?

options.text: So the budget is spent before the end of the year
So that each developer has exactly equal work
So that enablers and debt also get their share
So features can be built without any testing

questions.explanation: Capacity allocation reserves a share of capacity for enablers, maintenance and debt, so features do not crowd them out. It is a train-level policy, not an individual workload rule. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A feature in the backlog is too big for one PI. What should synthesize do?

options.text: Leave it whole and plan it across several PIs
Split it into smaller, valuable slices of work
Give it to the team with the most capacity
Turn it into a set of technical tasks by layer

questions.explanation: Features should fit in a PI, so large ones are split into smaller features that each deliver value and can be measured. Splitting by layer produces nothing usable. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who owns the ART backlog that synthesize feeds?

options.text: Product Management
The Business Owners
The System Architect
The Release Train Engineer

questions.explanation: Product Management owns and prioritises the ART backlog, with input from architects, Business Owners and teams. The RTE facilitates the train. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which items should reach PI Planning with acceptance criteria and a benefit hypothesis?

options.text: Each defect found in the last PI
Each epic in the portfolio backlog
Each feature planned for the PI
Each story in the team backlogs

questions.explanation: Features are the unit of PI Planning, so they arrive with benefit hypotheses and acceptance criteria. Stories are created from them by the teams. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does synthesize connect exploration to delivery?

options.text: It turns research into ranked features
It writes the release notes for customers
It approves the budget for each team
It hands the code to operations to deploy

questions.explanation: Synthesize turns what was learned and designed in exploration into a vision, roadmap and prioritised features that the train can plan and build. Deployment, budgets and release notes belong elsewhere. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · Synthesize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What happens in Continuous Integration?

options.text: Functionality is made available to chosen customers
Validated and integrated changes move from staging to production
New functionality is developed, tested, integrated and validated
Customer needs are researched and turned into features

questions.explanation: Continuous Integration is the pipeline aspect where functionality is developed, tested, integrated and validated ready for deployment. Moving changes from staging to production is Continuous Deployment. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Continuous Integration?

options.text: Deploy, verify, monitor, respond
Plan, code, review, merge
Build, deploy, release, measure
Develop, build, test end-to-end, stage

questions.explanation: The integration article lists develop, build, test end-to-end and stage. Deploy, verify, monitor and respond are the activities of Continuous Deployment. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: What does the build activity produce?

options.text: A production release for early customers
Deployable binaries, with branches merged into the trunk
Stories that are committed to version control
A staging environment that mirrors production in each detail

questions.explanation: Build creates deployable binaries and merges development branches into the trunk. Committing stories to version control belongs to the develop activity that precedes it. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: Engineers at Farrow Systems keep feature branches open for three weeks, and merges fail often. Which practice helps most?

options.text: A dedicated integrator who merges for the teams
Longer branches with a final review board
Trunk-based development with frequent small merges
A merge freeze until the end of the interval

questions.explanation: Short-lived branches merged into the trunk at least daily keep integration problems small. A dedicated integrator moves the pain to one person and leaves the batch size as large as before. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A change at Pell Digital breaks the main line for the whole train. Which practice would have stopped it reaching the trunk?

options.text: A weekly review of all the changes merged into the trunk
A rule that senior developers approve each merge by hand
A gated commit that runs the build and tests first
A larger staging environment

questions.explanation: Gated commits validate a change with an automated build and tests before it is merged into the trunk. A weekly review finds the break after everyone has already been blocked. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train at Osprey Rail integrates hardware and software from a supplier, and full integration is costly. What does SAFe advise?

options.text: Balance integration frequency, scope and testing cost
Integrate hourly whatever the cost
Exclude the supplier's parts from integration
Integrate once, shortly before the release date

questions.explanation: The integration article says such systems need an approach that balances frequency, the scope of integration and testing cost. Integrating once before release defers all the risk to the worst moment. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: During development at Halcyon Pay, the main line is often broken for days. Which integration principle is being missed?

options.text: The system should be running and potentially deployable throughout
The system should be rebuilt at the end of each interval
The system should be frozen before each demo
The system should be integrated by the System Team before each demo

questions.explanation: SAFe says the system should always run and be potentially deployable, even during development. Relying on the System Team to integrate makes integration someone else's job and delays feedback. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: A developer at Cobalt Travel writes a failing unit test, then the code to pass it, then tidies the design. Which practice is this?

options.text: Test-Driven Development
Behavior-Driven Development
Exploratory testing
Regression testing

questions.explanation: TDD builds and runs the test before the code it checks, then refactors. BDD also works test-first, but it specifies business-facing behaviour in scenarios. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Source: SAFe · Test-Driven Development.

questions.prompt: A product owner, a developer and a tester at Linden Health agree examples of how a refund should behave before coding starts. Which practice is this?

options.text: Pair programming
Test-Driven Development
Exploratory testing after each iteration
Behavior-Driven Development

questions.explanation: BDD creates shared understanding through business-facing scenarios defined before or with the specification of behaviour, using customer, development and test perspectives. TDD is the developer-level cycle on units of code. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Source: SAFe · Behavior-Driven Development.

questions.prompt: What mix of tests does a test-first approach tend to produce?

options.text: Many manual end-to-end tests and few unit tests
Few tests of any kind, written after release
Equal numbers of unit tests, integration tests and manual checks at each level
Many fast automated developer tests and fewer slow end-to-end tests

questions.explanation: Writing tests first gives a large base of fast automated tests and a smaller number of slow end-to-end ones, the shape of the testing pyramid. A suite that is mostly manual and end-to-end is slow and makes daily integration impractical. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Source: SAFe · Test-Driven Development.

questions.prompt: End-to-end tests at Thorne Bank fail because a partner's payment service is rarely available in test. Which technique helps?

options.text: Skipping payment tests until the partner is ready
Testing the payment flow in production alone
Asking the partner service team to pause its releases
Service virtualisation that simulates the partner service

questions.explanation: Service virtualisation stands in for systems that are unavailable or expensive to use, so end-to-end tests can run continuously. Skipping the tests removes feedback on one of the riskiest flows. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Tests pass before deployment at Rook Media but the same build fails when live. Which gap should the train close first?

options.text: Differences between test and production environments
Differences between story and feature estimates
Differences in the skills of testers and developers
Differences in the length of iterations

questions.explanation: Test results are trustworthy when test environments resemble production in configuration and data. Environment drift is a common reason a build that passed still fails once deployed. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the stage activity?

options.text: To collect usage data from customers
To host and validate the solution before production
To merge feature branches into the trunk
To release the solution to a first group of users

questions.explanation: Stage hosts and validates the solution in a staging environment before it goes to production. Releasing to a first group of users is a release decision, made after deployment. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: A train at Mistral Insurance keeps two identical production environments and switches traffic between them. Which technique is this?

options.text: Blue-green deployment
Canary release to early users
Feature toggle
Dark launch

questions.explanation: Blue-green deployment keeps an idle environment for the new version and switches traffic when it is ready, which also gives a fast way back. A canary release exposes the change to a small share of users first. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team at Ember Logistics stores application code in version control but keeps server configuration on a shared drive. What is the risk?

options.text: The trunk will hold too many small changes to review
Environments cannot be rebuilt reliably or audited
The System Demo will take longer
Developers will commit too frequently to the trunk each day

questions.explanation: Everything needed to build, test and deploy belongs in version control, including configuration and scripts. Without that, nobody can reproduce an environment or trace what changed before a failure. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Where does the train see integrated work from all teams each iteration?

options.text: At the PO Sync
At each team's iteration retrospective
At the Inspect and Adapt workshop alone
At the System Demo

questions.explanation: The System Demo shows the integrated work of all teams on the train, usually from a staging environment. Inspect and Adapt includes a demo too, but it happens once per planning interval. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Source: SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline.

questions.prompt: A team at Quill Bank wants to add static security analysis. Where in the pipeline does it give the fastest feedback?

options.text: In staging, once per interval
In the build, on each commit
In production, after release
In a review before the annual audit

questions.explanation: Automated scanning in the build tells the developer about a weakness minutes after writing it. Leaving it to staging or an audit lets vulnerable code spread before anyone knows. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for quality on an Agile team practising agile testing?

options.text: The testers on the team
The product owner
The System Team
The whole team

questions.explanation: Agile testing is collaborative, and all team members share responsibility for quality. Assigning it to testers alone brings back the handoff from developers to a test phase. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Source: SAFe · Agile Testing.

questions.prompt: Put the four activities of Continuous Integration in order.

options.text: Test end-to-end
Develop
Stage
Build

questions.explanation: Work is developed, built, tested end-to-end and then staged. Stage comes last because it validates the tested solution in a production-like environment before deployment. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: What does the develop activity of Continuous Integration cover?

options.text: Researching customer needs before features are defined
Turning stories into tested code, test-first
Deploying finished features to the production servers
Monitoring live systems for errors and slowdowns

questions.explanation: Develop splits features into stories and implements them with practices such as test-first, pairing and frequent commits. Research belongs to exploration and monitoring to deployment. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: Which practice keeps developers' changes small and integrated often?

options.text: Committing to the main branch at least daily
Working on private branches for a whole PI
Asking a lead to merge changes once a week
Merging all changes at the end of each iteration

questions.explanation: Frequent commits to a shared main branch keep each change small and expose conflicts early. Long-lived branches and batched merges delay integration. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does pair work help the develop activity?

options.text: It removes the need for code review and tests
Two people catch defects early and share knowledge
It halves the time needed to write each new feature
It lets one person work while the other rests

questions.explanation: Pairing gives continuous review and spreads knowledge of the code and practices. It does not halve the cost or replace automated tests. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A developer finishes a story's code but has written no tests. Under SAFe's test-first approach, what is wrong?

options.text: The code should be deployed before testing
The story should be sent to a separate test team
Nothing, since tests can be written next iteration
Tests should have shaped the code from the start

questions.explanation: Test-first means tests are written before or with the code, guiding the design and proving behaviour. Tests added later, or by someone else, lose that benefit. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is version control's role in Continuous Integration?

options.text: A database of the team's working hours
A store for the release notes of each version of the product
A tool that writes code from user stories
A single, shared source of truth for all changes

questions.explanation: Everything needed to build and run the solution, including code, tests, configuration and infrastructure, lives in version control, so builds are reproducible and changes traceable. It does not write code or record working hours. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which coding practice makes it safe to merge unfinished work into the main branch?

options.text: Leaving out the unit tests until it is done
Merging it at night when nobody is working
Copying it into a separate repository
Hiding it behind a feature toggle

questions.explanation: A toggle keeps unfinished functionality switched off while the code is integrated and tested with everything else. Skipping tests or hiding work elsewhere delays integration. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should the develop activity include building in security?

options.text: Flaws fixed while coding cost far less than later
Security teams are not allowed to review code
Secure code needs no testing in later stages
Security is required only for public websites

questions.explanation: Secure coding practices and early checks catch vulnerabilities when they are cheapest to fix. Later stages still test security; continuous security spreads it across the pipeline. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which story is best sized for the develop activity?

options.text: One that a team can finish within an iteration
One that covers a full feature in a single item
One that spans the whole PI for several teams
One that is estimated in months rather than days

questions.explanation: Small stories flow through develop, build and test quickly and give fast feedback. Features are split into several stories. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a code review for in Continuous Integration?

options.text: Catching problems early and spreading knowledge
Deciding which features to build next quarter
Approving the developer's annual performance rating
Replacing the need for automated tests entirely

questions.explanation: Reviews find defects and design issues before merge and share understanding across the team. They complement automated tests rather than replacing them. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Developers wait two days for a shared test database. Which improvement helps the develop activity most?

options.text: Self-service, disposable test environments
Testing directly against the live production data
Sharing one database among more teams
Booking the database a week in advance

questions.explanation: On-demand, disposable environments remove the wait and the conflicts of shared ones. Testing on live data creates privacy and stability risks. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does trunk-based development reduce integration risk?

options.text: Branches stay separate for good, so conflicts cannot occur
Small changes merge often, so conflicts stay small
Senior developers alone may commit to the trunk
Integration is moved to the end of each PI

questions.explanation: When everyone merges small changes to one trunk frequently, conflicts are small and found at once. Separate branches only postpone the conflicts. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Develop”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A build takes forty minutes, so developers stop running it before committing. What should the team do?

options.text: Add more manual checks to make up for it
Speed it up with caching and parallel tests
Let developers skip the build when they are busy
Run the build once a night instead of on each commit

questions.explanation: Fast builds keep developers running them on every change. Running the build less often delays feedback and lets defects pile up. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a gated commit?

options.text: A change that merges only if the build and tests pass
A commit that a manager must approve by email
A commit made on a locked branch at night
A change that is held until the end of the PI

questions.explanation: A gated commit runs the build and tests before the change reaches the main line, so the shared branch stays working. Manager approval and delays do not test anything. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which check belongs in the build activity on each commit?

options.text: A security audit by an external firm
Unit tests and static code analysis
A manual review of the release notes
Full user acceptance testing by the business

questions.explanation: Fast automated checks such as unit tests and static analysis run on every commit. Acceptance testing and audits are slower and run elsewhere or less often. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why must the main branch be fixed at once when the build breaks?

options.text: Broken builds are reported to the auditors each week
Everyone builds on it, so a break blocks all
Managers rate teams by how often their builds break
The break will fix itself after a few more commits

questions.explanation: A broken main line stops other teams integrating and testing their work, so fixing or reverting it comes first. Further commits make the cause harder to find. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice makes a build reproducible on any machine?

options.text: Keeping the build steps in a developer's notes
Declaring all dependencies and versions in code
Using the latest version of every library available
Installing tools by hand on each build server

questions.explanation: Pinned dependencies and build scripts in version control produce the same result everywhere. Hand-installed tools and floating versions cause 'works on my machine' failures. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a build artefact?

options.text: A server used only for running builds
A note describing what changed in the build
The packaged output of a build, ready to deploy
A defect found by the build process in the source code

questions.explanation: An artefact, such as a container image or package, is the versioned output that moves through the pipeline. Building it once keeps every environment identical. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which principle says the same artefact should move through every environment?

options.text: Build late, deploy early
Build per environment, deploy once
Build often, deploy rarely
Build once, deploy many

questions.explanation: Building one artefact and promoting it through test, staging and production means what was tested is what is deployed. Rebuilding per environment risks differences. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should builds run on every commit rather than once a day?

options.text: Commits are saved when a build runs
Daily builds are too slow for modern languages
Each failure then points to one small change
Builds on each commit can skip the tests

questions.explanation: When each commit is built and tested, a failure identifies the change that caused it. A daily build mixes many changes and makes diagnosis slow. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which tool scans a build for known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries?

options.text: A load and performance testing tool
An automatic code formatter for C#
A burn-down chart for the iteration
Software composition analysis

questions.explanation: Software composition analysis checks dependencies against databases of known vulnerabilities and licences. It belongs in the build as part of continuous security. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does continuous integration mean at the level of the whole system, beyond one team?

options.text: Letting a separate team integrate the work later
Integrating the system just before each release
Each team integrating its own code once per PI
Frequently merging each team's work as one

questions.explanation: System-level integration brings every team's work together frequently, ideally continuously, so the train sees a working solution. Integrating late hides problems until release. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team's builds pass, but they take days to reach a shared integration environment. What does this delay?

options.text: The team's iteration planning for the next sprint
The writing of release notes by product marketing
The licence renewal for the build tools
Feedback on how the work fits with other teams'

questions.explanation: A team-level build proves the team's code; only system integration shows whether it works with everything else. Delay there postpones the most important feedback. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Build”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the test end-to-end activity check?

options.text: That the release has been approved by the business
That each developer's code compiles on their machine
That the marketing material matches the features
That the integrated solution works as a whole

questions.explanation: Test end-to-end validates the integrated solution, including functional behaviour and nonfunctional requirements, in a production-like setting. Compiling is part of build. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: End-to-end tests often fail for reasons unrelated to the code under test. What should the team do first?

options.text: Rerun failing tests until they eventually pass
Delete the end-to-end tests that fail most often
Ignore the failures and release anyway
Find and fix the causes of flaky tests

questions.explanation: Flaky tests destroy trust in the suite, so their causes, such as timing, shared data or unstable environments, are fixed first. Reruns and deletion hide real defects. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe include nonfunctional testing in test end-to-end?

options.text: Only operations cares about nonfunctional needs
Nonfunctional needs are checked by customers
System qualities can regress with any change
Nonfunctional testing is cheaper than unit testing

questions.explanation: Performance, security and reliability are constraints on the whole system, and any change can break them, so they are tested continuously like functional behaviour. Leaving them to the end hides regressions until release. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Source: SAFe · Nonfunctional Requirements.

questions.prompt: Which test data practice best supports end-to-end testing?

options.text: Realistic, anonymised data created on demand
No data, since end-to-end tests need none
A few hand-typed records shared by all teams
A copy of live customer data with real names

questions.explanation: Realistic but anonymised data, generated or refreshed as needed, exercises the system properly without privacy risk. Shared hand-made records cause conflicts and gaps. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which kind of test checks a whole user journey through the system?

options.text: A static analysis check
A contract test
An end-to-end test
A unit test

questions.explanation: End-to-end tests drive complete journeys across components. Unit tests check small pieces, and contract tests check agreements between services. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train runs its full regression suite once, at the end of each PI. What does test end-to-end suggest?

options.text: Run it after each release in production
Run it twice at the end of each PI, just to be sure of it
Automate and run it continuously as changes arrive
Drop it, since unit tests catch everything

questions.explanation: Continuous, automated regression testing finds breakages soon after the change that caused them. Testing at the end of the PI finds them late, in a batch. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should end-to-end tests be fewer than unit tests?

options.text: They are slower and more brittle
End-to-end tests cannot find any real defects
End-to-end tests are banned in DevOps pipelines
Unit tests cover the whole user journey too

questions.explanation: The test pyramid keeps most checks in fast unit tests and a smaller number of end-to-end journeys, which keeps the pipeline quick and reliable. End-to-end tests still find defects that unit tests miss. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice checks that a change leaves working features intact?

options.text: A design review of the new code
User research with new customers
Automated regression testing
Exploratory testing of the new feature

questions.explanation: Regression tests re-run existing checks on every change to catch unintended breakage. Exploratory testing looks for new problems in new work. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is service virtualisation used for in testing?

options.text: Moving all servers into virtual machines
Turning off a service during a deployment
Charging teams for each test they run
Simulating slow or missing dependent services

questions.explanation: Virtual services stand in for partner systems that are costly, slow or unavailable, so end-to-end tests can run reliably. It is not about virtual machines. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do end-to-end tests run in a production-like environment?

options.text: Production-like environments are cheaper than laptops
Auditors require a copy of production for testing
Tests in production-like systems never fail
Differences hide defects until release

questions.explanation: If the test environment differs from production in versions, configuration or data, defects stay hidden until the solution goes live. Matching environments makes test results meaningful. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Test end-to-end”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which activity follows test end-to-end in Continuous Integration?

options.text: Stage
Deploy
Build
Verify

questions.explanation: Continuous Integration runs develop, build, test end-to-end, then stage. Deploy and verify belong to Continuous Deployment. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: The staging environment uses different database and runtime versions from production. What is the risk?

options.text: The build will refuse to run in either environment
Staging becomes faster than production over time
Issues appear only after deployment to production
Developers cannot log in to the staging servers

questions.explanation: Staging is meant to predict production behaviour; when versions differ, it cannot, and problems surface live. Environments built from the same code avoid this. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should staging be built from the same code as production?

options.text: So it can replace production during a busy period
So it behaves like production and can be trusted
So auditors do not need to see production at all
So that developers can use it as a backup system

questions.explanation: Infrastructure and configuration as code let staging mirror production, so a successful staging run is real evidence. It is not a backup or a spare. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Where does a train show the integrated increment to stakeholders each iteration?

options.text: The monthly portfolio sync meeting
The System Demo, often from staging
A breakout during PI Planning
The team retrospective each iteration

questions.explanation: The System Demo shows the integrated increment of all teams, often running in staging, so stakeholders see real progress. Retrospectives and portfolio syncs serve other purposes. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does infrastructure as code give the stage activity?

options.text: Code that runs faster in production than in test
A list of the team's hardware purchases
Environments that can be rebuilt exactly and often
Servers that need no security updates at all

questions.explanation: Defining environments in versioned code lets teams create identical, disposable staging environments on demand. Patching still happens, through the code. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team wants a staging environment available on demand for each feature. What makes this practical?

options.text: A shared spreadsheet for booking the environment
Automated provisioning from code
A larger single staging server for all teams
A queue of requests handled by the operations team

questions.explanation: Automated provisioning from code makes environments cheap to create and destroy, so each feature can have one. Queues and bookings keep the wait. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is staging a key step before Continuous Deployment?

options.text: It is the only place where code is compiled
It proves it works in production-like conditions
It replaces the need to monitor production
It lets marketing preview features before release

questions.explanation: Staging gives the last high-confidence check before production, in an environment that matches it. Monitoring is still needed after deployment. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Stage”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does Continuous Deployment do?

options.text: Makes new functionality visible to all customers
Automates moving functionality from staging to production
Decides which features customers will receive
Integrates code from all teams into the trunk

questions.explanation: Continuous Deployment automates the migration of functionality from staging into production, where it becomes available for release. Making it visible to customers is a separate release decision. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Continuous Deployment?

options.text: Release, stabilize, measure, learn
Stage, deploy, release, support
Develop, build, test end-to-end, stage
Deploy, verify, monitor, respond

questions.explanation: The deployment article lists deploy, verify, monitor and respond. Release, stabilize, measure and learn belong to Release on Demand. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe separate deployment from release?

options.text: Developers can skip testing in the staging environment
Releases can be bundled into fewer, larger events
Changes can reach production without changing what users see
Operations can approve each change before it is built

questions.explanation: With deployment separate from release, functionality sits in production, verified, until the business chooses to turn it on. Bundling releases into larger events is the opposite of the small batches this enables. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: A team at Aldous Retail deploys a new pricing engine to production but keeps it switched off for customers. Which technique allows this?

options.text: A blue-green switch of all traffic
A gated commit
A rollback
A feature toggle

questions.explanation: A feature toggle lets deployed code stay hidden until it is switched on, for everyone or for chosen users. A blue-green switch changes the whole environment and does not hide one feature inside it. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: At Sorrel Bank, a new fraud model runs in production on live traffic, and its results are recorded but not used. What is this called?

options.text: A dark launch
A system demo
A hotfix
A canary release

questions.explanation: A dark launch puts functionality into production without exposing it to users, so the team can see how it behaves under real conditions. A canary release does expose the change, to a small group of users. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the verify activity?

options.text: To confirm the business owners approve the release
To confirm the build compiles without warnings
To confirm changes work in production before customers see them
To confirm stories meet their acceptance criteria in test

questions.explanation: Verify checks that changes operate in production as intended before they are released to customers. Checking acceptance criteria in a test environment happens earlier, in integration. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Which practice supports the verify activity?

options.text: Automated production tests run after each deployment
A weekly meeting of the change board
A user acceptance phase held before the staging environment
A survey sent to customers after release

questions.explanation: Automated tests in production confirm that the deployed change behaves correctly in its real environment. A change board meeting adds delay and tells nobody whether the change works. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the monitor activity cover?

options.text: Auditing commits for coding standards
Reviewing features with the business owners
Tracking team velocity across iterations
Watching production and reporting on issues

questions.explanation: Monitor means observing the production environment and reporting on any issues. It concerns the health of the running solution, not the progress of the teams. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Operations at Tidewater Energy see server metrics, but nobody can tell whether a new feature is being used. What is missing?

options.text: Full-stack telemetry that includes business measures
A longer period of testing in staging
A larger operations team on each shift
A second monitoring tool for the servers and the network

questions.explanation: Full-stack telemetry collects data from infrastructure up to feature usage and business results, so technical and business questions can both be answered. A second server tool repeats the view the train already has. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the respond activity mean?

options.text: Addressing problems rapidly when they occur
Replying to audit findings each quarter
Reporting status to the portfolio
Answering customer feature requests

questions.explanation: Respond is the ability to address problems rapidly when they arise in deployment and production. It is about incidents, not about requests for new functionality. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: A deployment at Garnet Travel causes errors for a tenth of users. The team can undo the change in two minutes or write a fix in about an hour. Which reasoning fits?

options.text: Leave the change live and fix it within the hour
Wait for the next planned deployment window
Call a change board to decide the next step
Roll back now to restore service, then fix the cause

questions.explanation: Restoring service fast is the priority, and a two-minute rollback does that while the team works on the cause. Fixing forward is reasonable when it is quicker or rollback is unsafe, which is not the case here. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Servers at Bexley Insurance are patched by hand and have drifted apart, so deployments behave differently on each. Which practice removes the drift?

options.text: Immutable infrastructure rebuilt from versioned definitions
A monthly meeting to compare settings
A detailed manual that describes the settings of each server
A freeze on changes to the servers

questions.explanation: With immutable infrastructure, servers are replaced from definitions held in version control and are never changed in place, so each one matches. A manual describes the intended state but cannot enforce it. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train at Larch Pay deploys by hand once a month. Leaders say automation is too costly. Which economic argument does SAFe make?

options.text: Automation pays back when releases become larger
Automation removes the need for monitoring
Automation lowers transaction cost, so small batches pay off
Automation raises quality so far that staging tests can be dropped

questions.explanation: The deployment article says teams reduce the transaction cost and risk of moving changes to production by automating, which makes small batches worthwhile. Automation does not replace testing or monitoring; it makes them repeatable. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: A product manager at Onyx Media wants to compare two versions of a sign-up page with real users. What makes this possible?

options.text: A manual switch performed during a change window
A longer staging period, so both versions are tested by the whole train
Deployment separated from release, so each group sees one version
A second production release, scheduled for next month

questions.explanation: Separating deployment from release allows experiments such as A/B tests, because functionality can be shown to chosen users. Staging has no real customers, so it cannot answer which version they prefer. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Developers at Finch Health must raise a ticket and wait two days for operations to deploy to a test environment. Which practice removes the queue?

options.text: A form with more detail on each request
A weekly slot reserved for test deployments
A second operations engineer assigned to handle the tickets
Self-service deployment through the automated pipeline

questions.explanation: Self-service deployment lets teams trigger a controlled, automated deployment themselves, which removes the wait. Another engineer shortens the queue for a while but keeps the handoff. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An incident review at Wexford Bank ends by naming the engineer who ran the failed command. What is wrong with that outcome?

options.text: It leaves out the cost of the incident
It should have been decided by the change board, not the team
It hides the system causes and discourages open reporting
It should also name the engineer's manager

questions.explanation: A blameless review looks for the conditions that allowed the failure, so the system can be improved. Naming a person teaches people to conceal problems, which slows detection next time. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice lets a train send a change to one region before the rest?

options.text: Service virtualisation
Trunk-based development
Selective deployment
Gated commit

questions.explanation: Selective deployment sends a change to specific environments or segments first, which limits the effect of a problem. The other options are integration practices that act before deployment. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team at Ridgeway Rail notices rising memory use and replaces the instance before users are affected. Which capability is this?

options.text: Proactive detection
Dark launch
Session replay
Canary release

questions.explanation: Proactive detection finds problems before they cause an outage, often through telemetry and deliberate fault testing. Session replay helps to understand a problem after a user has already met it. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Put the four activities of Continuous Deployment in order.

options.text: Verify
Deploy
Monitor
Respond

questions.explanation: The solution is deployed, verified in production, monitored and then problems are responded to. Verify precedes monitor because the team first confirms the change works before watching it over time. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Which activity starts the CD aspect of the pipeline?

options.text: Deploy
Verify
Stage
Monitor

questions.explanation: Continuous Deployment runs deploy, verify, monitor and respond. Stage is the last activity of Continuous Integration. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: A team deploys to production by running scripts by hand from a checklist. What should it change?

options.text: Deploy less often to reduce the manual effort
Add a second person to read out the checklist
Automate the deployment through the pipeline
Move the scripts into a shared document folder

questions.explanation: Automated, repeatable deployment removes manual errors and makes frequent deployment cheap. Deploying less often makes each one bigger and riskier. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do smaller, more frequent deployments lower risk?

options.text: Small changes make failures easy to find and fix
Frequent deployments are approved more quickly
Smaller deployments use less server memory
Small deployments need no testing at all

questions.explanation: Each small deployment changes little, so if something goes wrong, the cause is obvious and rollback is easy. Large, rare deployments combine many risks. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a dark launch?

options.text: Releasing a feature with the logging turned off
Deploying only at night to avoid users
Launching a feature with no documentation
Running a feature live but hidden from users

questions.explanation: A dark launch deploys a feature to production and exercises it, for example with real traffic, without exposing it to users. It tests production behaviour safely. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice lets a team deploy database changes without breaking the running version?

options.text: Backward-compatible schema changes made in steps
Dropping old columns before deploying the new code
Locking the database during every deployment
Asking users to log out during the change

questions.explanation: Expand-and-contract changes add new structures first, migrate, then remove old ones later, so old and new code both work during the deployment. Dropping columns first breaks the version still running. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe want deployment to be a low-ceremony technical event?

options.text: So managers no longer need to know about releases
So changes can flow often and safely
So business decisions can be made by developers
So the change board can meet less often

questions.explanation: When deploying is routine and automated, changes reach production continuously, and release remains a separate business decision. The aim is flow, not fewer meetings. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A deployment needs a two-hour outage each time. Which technique removes the outage?

options.text: Deploying only on public holidays
Announcing the outage further in advance
Reducing the number of servers deployed
Blue-green deployment with a traffic switch

questions.explanation: Blue-green deployment prepares the new version beside the old one and switches traffic, so there is no outage and rollback is a switch back. Holidays and notices only move the outage. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In a mature DevOps train, who should be able to deploy to production?

options.text: The tool vendor, during its own support window
The operations team alone, after a ticket is raised
The team, through an automated, governed pipeline
Any manager who approves the change by email

questions.explanation: Self-service deployment through a pipeline with built-in controls removes handoffs while keeping governance. Ticket queues add days of waiting. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Deploy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question does the verify activity answer?

options.text: Does the change meet the customer's real need?
Has the change been approved by the board?
Does the change work correctly in production?
Is the change ready to be merged into main?

questions.explanation: Verify confirms that the deployed change works in production before it affects users. Whether it meets the need is measured after release. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Right after a deployment, a team runs a small set of automated checks against production. What are these?

options.text: Unit tests
Usability tests
Smoke tests
Load tests

questions.explanation: Smoke tests are quick checks that the main functions work after a deployment. Unit tests ran long before, and load and usability tests serve other purposes. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why test in production as well as before it?

options.text: Production tests replace the need for staging
Testing before production is not allowed in DevOps
Some issues show only with real traffic and data
Customers prefer to find defects themselves

questions.explanation: Real traffic, data and configuration reveal problems that no test environment can fully reproduce. Production testing complements earlier testing. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice limits the impact if a production test finds a problem?

options.text: Testing during the busiest hour of the day
Testing with all users at once, to be thorough
Testing with a small share of traffic first
Testing just after the press release goes out

questions.explanation: Exposing a change to a small share of traffic first, as in a canary, limits how many users a problem can reach. Testing at peak or with everyone maximises harm. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does the verify activity handle test data in production?

options.text: Leaves the test records mixed with real ones
Copies real customer data into the test accounts
Deletes all production data after each test
Uses masked or synthetic data, then cleans up

questions.explanation: Production tests use clearly marked synthetic or masked data and remove it afterwards, so customers and reports are not affected. Real customer data must not be copied into tests. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A deployment passes smoke tests, but a key business transaction fails for one customer type. Which verify practice would have caught it?

options.text: Checks of critical journeys for each user segment
A longer wait before the next deployment
A check that the server's CPU is below 80%
A manual review of the deployment script

questions.explanation: Verification should cover the critical business journeys, including important variations, not just that the system is up. Server checks miss business failures. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What should happen if verification fails right after a deployment?

options.text: Release the feature to users to collect more data
Log the failure and review it at the next PI
Wait a day to see whether the failure clears itself
Roll back or fix forward at once

questions.explanation: A failed verification means the change is not fit for users, so it is reversed or fixed at once. Waiting or releasing spreads the harm. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In which environment does the verify activity work?

options.text: Staging
Test
Production
Development

questions.explanation: Verify takes place after deployment, in production, which is what distinguishes it from the testing done in Continuous Integration. Staging, development and test come before it. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice lets a team verify a feature with internal staff before customers see it?

options.text: Asking staff to imagine using it
Deploying it to a laptop for testing
Writing release notes for the staff
Toggling it on for employees only

questions.explanation: Feature toggles can expose a deployed feature to a chosen group, such as employees, for real use in production before release. Laptops and imagined use are not real use. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should verification be automated?

options.text: So the tests run only once a month
So each deployment is checked fast, alike
So that verification can be skipped on busy days
So the operations team can be removed altogether

questions.explanation: Automated verification runs consistently on every deployment and gives fast feedback, which frequent deployment needs. Manual checks are slow and vary. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Verify”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is full-stack telemetry?

options.text: A dashboard that shows only server CPU and memory
A report of all incidents in the last year
A complete list of the team's monitoring tools
Data from infrastructure, apps and business use

questions.explanation: Full-stack telemetry collects data across the infrastructure, application and business layers, so teams can see both technical health and value. CPU alone misses most of it. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Which measure tells a team whether a newly released feature is delivering value?

options.text: The number of lines of code in the feature
The time it took to write the release notes
The CPU load on the servers that run it
Business metrics such as feature usage

questions.explanation: Value shows in business measures, such as usage and conversion, tied to the feature's hypothesis. Server load and code size are not value. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should monitoring alert on user impact as well as on server metrics?

options.text: Alerts on servers are banned by most regulators
Server metrics cannot be collected in the cloud
Users can suffer even when servers look healthy
Users report problems faster than any alert

questions.explanation: Failed transactions, slow pages and errors can occur while CPU and memory look normal, so alerts tied to user experience catch what infrastructure alerts miss. Users should not have to be the alert. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team's dashboards raise hundreds of alerts a day, and engineers ignore them. What should it do?

options.text: Hire more engineers to read the alerts
Add more alerts so important events are caught
Tune alerts so each one needs action
Turn off alerting until there is time to review it

questions.explanation: Alert fatigue makes real problems invisible; fewer, meaningful alerts that need action restore their value. More alerts or more readers make it worse. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of logging in the monitor activity?

options.text: Recording events so problems can be diagnosed
Recording who approved each deployment
Recording the hours spent on each story
Recording the team's attendance at events

questions.explanation: Structured logs record what the system did, which is essential for diagnosing incidents. Approvals and hours are management data. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps a team trace one slow request across several services?

options.text: Code coverage
Weekly status reports
Manual log reading
Distributed tracing

questions.explanation: Distributed tracing follows a request through each service with a shared identifier, showing where time is spent. Reading logs by hand across services is slow and error-prone. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should teams monitor the business effect of a release as well as its technical health?

options.text: Technical health cannot be measured in production
Business effects are monitored by finance alone
Monitoring business effects removes the need for tests
It can run perfectly and still deliver no value

questions.explanation: A technically healthy feature may not change customer behaviour; business telemetry shows whether the hypothesis held, which feeds the learn activity. Technical health is still monitored too. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which monitoring practice best supports the measure activity of Release on Demand?

options.text: Disk-space alerts on the database servers
A log of the team's on-call rota
Telemetry on how users use features
A count of the deployments made each month

questions.explanation: Measuring a release's value needs data on real feature use, which monitoring must capture. Disk alerts and deployment counts are operational data. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a service level objective?

options.text: A list of the servers a service runs on
A goal for the number of features released
A contract that names the team's vendor
A target for a measure of service reliability

questions.explanation: An SLO sets a target, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding, for a service level indicator. It guides alerting and how much risk a team can take with changes. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Memory use on a service climbs steadily after each deployment. What does good monitoring enable?

options.text: Spotting the trend and acting early
Waiting until the service crashes to investigate
Restarting all services every hour as a habit
Doubling the memory without finding the cause

questions.explanation: Trends in telemetry give early warning, so the team can find the leak and fix it before an outage. Restarts and more memory hide the cause. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is monitoring designed in during exploration and development as well as at release?

options.text: Useful telemetry depends on how the code is built
Monitoring tools are only sold to development teams
Release teams cannot install monitoring tools
Monitoring replaces the need for testing

questions.explanation: Meaningful logs, metrics and traces have to be built into the code and architecture. Bolting monitoring on at release leaves gaps. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Monitor”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An incident affects customers. What is the first priority in the respond activity?

options.text: Wait for the next release to include a fix
Write the full incident report before acting
Find the person responsible before fixing anything
Restore service, then find the root cause

questions.explanation: Respond puts restoring service first, through rollback, failover or a quick fix, then investigates causes. Blame and paperwork delay recovery. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does mean time to recover measure?

options.text: How long a team spends in planning events
How often deployments cause incidents
How long a feature takes from idea to release
How fast service is restored after failure

questions.explanation: Mean time to recover tracks how quickly service is restored after an incident, a key DevOps measure. Change failure rate tracks how often deployments cause incidents. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe favour blameless post-incident reviews?

options.text: People speak openly, so system causes get fixed
Reviews are faster when no one is blamed
Blameless reviews mean nobody is accountable
Blame is required by most audit standards

questions.explanation: When people are not punished, they explain what really happened, which reveals the system causes behind incidents. Accountability shifts to fixing the system. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A defect is found in production. Which approach fixes it fastest and most safely?

options.text: Wait for the next scheduled quarterly release
Patch the production server by hand straight away
Ask users to work around the defect for now
Fix forward through the normal automated pipeline

questions.explanation: A fast pipeline lets a small fix go through the same tests and deployment as any change. Manual patches cause drift and new errors. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a runbook?

options.text: A report of all incidents from the last year
The source code of the deployment pipeline
A list of runners for the company sports day
Steps for handling a known operational issue

questions.explanation: A runbook documents how to diagnose and resolve a known type of issue, ideally automated over time. It speeds response and reduces errors under pressure. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps a team respond quickly to a problem that only one customer reports?

options.text: Logs and telemetry filtered by customer
Ask the customer to reinstall the software
Roll back every release from the last month
Ignore it until more customers report it

questions.explanation: Telemetry and logs that can be filtered by customer let the team find a narrow problem quickly. Mass rollbacks are out of proportion. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should incident findings feed back into the backlog?

options.text: So incidents are counted in the team's velocity
So fixes for causes are prioritised like other work
So that the team that caused it is shown publicly
So the incident can be hidden from the Business Owners

questions.explanation: Root-cause fixes compete for capacity like any other work; putting them in the backlog makes sure they are planned rather than forgotten. Hiding or blaming defeats the purpose. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice checks how a system copes with failures before real ones happen?

options.text: More frequent status meetings
Fewer and larger deployments
Longer and more detailed code reviews
Chaos engineering experiments

questions.explanation: Chaos engineering injects controlled failures to test resilience and response, so weaknesses are fixed before real incidents. Reviews and meetings do not test the running system. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the role of on-call in the respond activity?

options.text: A schedule for deploying code at night only
A meeting where incidents are assigned blame
A rota for answering customer sales questions
A named person ready to act quickly

questions.explanation: On-call means someone with the skills and access is ready to respond at any time. In DevOps, the team that builds a service often shares its on-call. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.
