questions.prompt: How does fast response support release on demand?

options.text: Quick fixes make frequent release safer
Release on demand means problems are ignored
Fast response is required only for large releases
Fast response removes the need for any testing

questions.explanation: When problems can be detected and fixed quickly, the cost of a bad release falls, so the business can release more often with confidence. Testing is still needed before each release. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Respond”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is Release on Demand?

options.text: Releasing each change to all customers as soon as it passes its last test
Releasing all features at the end of a planning interval
Releasing functionality at once or in increments, as the business needs
Releasing when operations has capacity to support it

questions.explanation: Release on Demand makes functionality available immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs. Releasing each change the moment it passes tests ignores the business decision about timing. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which four activities belong to Release on Demand?

options.text: Deploy, verify, monitor, respond
Stage, release, monitor, improve
Release, stabilize, measure, learn
Plan, release, support, retire

questions.explanation: The study guide lists releasing value, stabilising the solution, measuring business value and learning from feedback. Deploy, verify, monitor and respond are the deployment activities that come before. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Source: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: SDP (6.0).

questions.prompt: Who decides when a feature is released to customers?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer with the System Team
Product Management with the business owners
The operations lead on call
The team that built the feature

questions.explanation: The release article says Product Management and business owners decide when to release, which features and to whom. The team makes deployment routine, but the timing of release is a business decision. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: A feature at Halyard Retail is deployed and verified in September, but marketing wants to launch it with a November campaign. What does SAFe allow?

options.text: Remove it from production until November
Delay all other deployments until November
Release it now, since it is ready
Keep it deployed and release it in November

questions.explanation: Because release is decoupled from deployment, the business can choose a release date that suits market rhythms and campaigns. Removing working code from production adds risk and gains nothing. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: A team at Pallas Bank shows a new transfer screen to two percent of customers and watches the error rate before widening it. Which technique is this?

options.text: A gated commit
A dark launch
A blue-green deployment
A canary release

questions.explanation: A canary release exposes a change to a small group of real users and expands as confidence grows. A dark launch runs in production without users seeing it at all. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A solution at Seaton Telecom has a web front end, an API and a billing engine that are always released together. What would SAFe suggest?

options.text: Release the billing engine first and the rest a year later
Merge the three elements into one component
Decouple the elements so each can release independently
Give all three the cadence of the slowest element

questions.explanation: Decoupling release elements lets parts of the solution reach customers at the pace each market needs. Tying everything to the slowest element delays value that is ready now. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the aim of the stabilize activity?

options.text: Freezing changes until the next planning interval
Reducing the number of features in the release
Completing the tests that were skipped earlier in the interval
Keeping the released solution reliable, secure and available

questions.explanation: Stabilize makes sure the solution keeps meeting its nonfunctional requirements in operation, with practices such as failover and continuous security monitoring. It is not a hardening phase for unfinished testing. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A region fails at Kelso Health and traffic moves to a second region without users noticing. Which stabilize practice does this show?

options.text: Innovation accounting and leading indicators
Threat modelling
Feature toggles
Failover and disaster recovery

questions.explanation: Failover and disaster recovery are designed and rehearsed so the service survives the loss of a component or site. Threat modelling is a design-time security practice used in exploration. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A feature at Briar Travel was released with the expectation that it would raise repeat bookings. What does the measure activity do?

options.text: Counts the story points the feature took
Compares actual results with the benefit hypothesis
Records how many defects were fixed
Confirms the feature passed its acceptance tests

questions.explanation: Measure evaluates whether the released functionality delivers the benefit that was predicted, using the indicators chosen during exploration. Passing acceptance tests shows the feature was built as specified, not that it was worth building. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What happens to what the train learns after a release?

options.text: It is kept by Product Management until the next year
It is reported to operations for future support
It is archived with the release notes
It feeds back into Continuous Exploration

questions.explanation: The release article says the activities of Release on Demand feed back into exploration, which closes the loop of the pipeline. Archiving the learning breaks the loop and the next hypothesis starts from guesswork. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand; SAFe · Continuous Exploration.

questions.prompt: Results at Morven Foods show a released feature has no effect on orders. Which options does Lean startup thinking offer?

options.text: Add more features until orders rise
Remove the measures that show no effect
Hand the feature to another train
Pivot, persevere with changes, or stop

questions.explanation: The learn activity uses the evidence to decide whether to pivot, persevere or stop. Adding features without a new hypothesis spends more on an idea the data has not supported. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Castell Insurance say release on demand means every team must release daily. What is the best correction?

options.text: Release frequency follows the length of the iteration
Release frequency is fixed at once per planning interval for each train
Release frequency follows business need, which differs by solution
Release frequency is set by the slowest team

questions.explanation: On demand means the business can release when it wants to, whether that is many times a day or a few times a year. The planning interval is a cadence for planning and does not dictate release timing. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does decoupling release from deployment give the sales and marketing groups?

options.text: Control of the team backlog
Confidence to schedule launches and promotions
Access to the staging environment
The authority to approve or reject each deployment

questions.explanation: The release article notes that decoupling lets marketing target promotions and sales schedule with confidence. They gain predictability of release timing, not a role in approving deployments. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: After a release at Ostrander Pay, the team runs a value stream mapping session on its own pipeline. Which activity is this part of?

options.text: Verify
Learn
Stabilize
Release

questions.explanation: Learn includes relentless improvement of the pipeline itself, and mapping the value stream again shows where the next delay sits. Stabilize keeps the running solution healthy and does not examine the delivery process. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each activity to its aspect of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

options.text: Continuous Integration
Continuous Deployment
Value Stream Mapping
Release on Demand
Continuous Exploration

questions.explanation: Synthesize ends exploration, stage ends integration, verify follows deploy, and stabilize follows release. Value stream mapping is a technique for improving the pipeline and is not one of its four aspects. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline; Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: SDP (6.0); SAFe · Continuous Integration; SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Which technique releases a deployed feature to a growing share of users over several days?

options.text: A progressive rollout behind toggles
A separate branch kept for each user group
A single big-bang launch to every user
A code freeze until the marketing date

questions.explanation: Toggles or routing let the business widen exposure step by step while watching the measures, and pull back if needed. A big-bang launch exposes everyone to any problem at once. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe say different parts of a solution may be released on different cadences?

options.text: The parts with the most code should be released more often
Release cadence is set by the PI calendar for each part
Each part has its own market needs and its own risks
Each part must be released on the same day for safety

questions.explanation: A mobile app, an API and a billing engine may need different release rhythms. Architecture that lets them release separately gives the business that choice. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which item must be ready, besides working code, before a feature is released?

options.text: Compliance, security and support readiness
A full rewrite of the user manual from the start
A new version of the team's working agreement
A sign-off from every developer on the train

questions.explanation: Release governance covers compliance, security, documentation and support readiness, so the release is safe and supported. A full manual rewrite and universal sign-offs are not required. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A regulated firm must keep a record of what was released and when. Which practice supports this without slowing releases?

options.text: A monthly meeting to approve all releases
A paper form signed for each change
Automated audit trails from the pipeline
A rule to release once a year

questions.explanation: The pipeline can record each build, test, approval and release automatically, which satisfies auditors and keeps flow fast. Meetings and paper forms add delay. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Release”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the stabilize activity of Release on Demand aim for?

options.text: A slower release cadence to reduce change in production
A solution that stays usable, secure and recoverable
A smaller set of features than was first planned
A frozen code base that no team may change for a PI

questions.explanation: Stabilize keeps the released solution working well, available, secure and recoverable, so users get its value. Freezing code and slowing releases are not the aim. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: Which practice keeps a service available if one of its servers fails?

options.text: A single larger server in one site
Redundancy with automatic failover
A manual restart guide for operators
A weekly backup kept off site

questions.explanation: Redundant instances with automatic failover keep the service running when one part fails. Backups help recovery but do not keep the service up. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is disaster recovery tested regularly rather than only planned?

options.text: Auditors will not read a plan that has not been tested
A tested plan removes the need for backups
Testing recovery is faster than writing the plan
Untested recovery plans often fail when needed

questions.explanation: Practising recovery shows whether backups restore, people know their roles and time targets are met. A plan on paper may hide gaps until a real disaster. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Traffic to a newly released feature is ten times higher than expected. Which stabilize practice helps most?

options.text: Automatic scaling of capacity to match demand
Turning off monitoring to save server resources
Asking users to come back at quieter times
Releasing a second feature to share the load

questions.explanation: Elastic, automatic scaling keeps response times acceptable when demand jumps. Turning off monitoring removes the view needed to manage the spike. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which security practice belongs in the stabilize activity?

options.text: Ongoing monitoring and patching for new threats
A yearly reminder email about password safety
A one-off penetration test before the first release
A rule that only managers may log in to production

questions.explanation: Threats change after release, so stabilize monitors and patches continuously. A one-off test and occasional reminders leave long gaps. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team must apply an urgent security patch to a released service. Which approach is safest?

options.text: Ask users to install the patch themselves
Use the normal fast pipeline and tests
Apply it by hand on each server at once
Wait for the next quarterly release window

questions.explanation: A fast, trusted pipeline lets even urgent fixes go through the usual tests and controls. Manual changes cause drift, and waiting leaves the risk open. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does architecting for operations support stabilize?

options.text: Releases can be made without any testing at all
Failover and telemetry designs make recovery easier
The solution never needs any further changes
Operations teams then need no access to production

questions.explanation: Designs that include redundancy, telemetry and safe deployment make the solution easier to keep stable and to recover. They do not remove the need for testing or change. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure shows how well the stabilize activity is working?

options.text: The length of the release notes
The number of features released this PI
Availability against its target
The number of developers on the team

questions.explanation: Availability and similar reliability measures, compared with targets, show whether the solution stays usable. Feature counts and team size are not stability measures. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Stabilize”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the measure activity of Release on Demand check?

options.text: Whether the code meets the team's style guide
Whether the release went out on the planned date
Whether the feature delivered its benefit
Whether the team met its story point estimates

questions.explanation: Measure compares real results with the feature's benefit hypothesis, using leading indicators and business outcomes. Estimates, dates and style are delivery concerns. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: A feature's benefit hypothesis expected 10% more returning customers. Which data does the measure activity need?

options.text: Repeat order rates, before and after
The number of commits made by the team
The time taken to deploy the feature
The number of tests written for the feature

questions.explanation: Measuring the hypothesis needs the outcome it named, compared with a baseline. Tests, commits and deployment time describe the work, not the result. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should the success measures for a feature be agreed before it is released?

options.text: Measures chosen late tend to flatter the result
Auditors check the date the measure was written
Telemetry can only be added before release
Measures cannot be changed after the PI starts

questions.explanation: Deciding the measures up front keeps the test honest and makes sure telemetry exists to collect them. Choosing them after the fact invites picking whatever looks good. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Two versions of a sign-up page are shown to random halves of users to see which converts better. What is this?

options.text: A/B testing
Load testing
Smoke testing
Regression testing

questions.explanation: A/B testing compares variants with real users at random to find which performs better. Smoke, load and regression tests check that the solution works. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which kind of measure arrives last and confirms whether a release created business value?

options.text: A build duration trend
A unit test pass rate
A leading indicator of usage
A lagging outcome

questions.explanation: Lagging outcomes, such as revenue or retention, arrive later but confirm the value. Leading indicators move early and help steer before then. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A released feature's usage is strong in one region and near zero in another. What should the measure activity do?

options.text: Remove the weaker region's data as an outlier
Report the average across regions as the result
Segment results by region and look for the cause
Roll the feature back everywhere straight away

questions.explanation: Segmenting results shows where the hypothesis holds and where it does not, which guides the next decision. An average hides the difference. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does the measure activity feed Continuous Exploration?

options.text: It sets the budget for the next financial year
Results show which hypotheses held, guiding ideas
It sends the code back to be rewritten from scratch
It replaces the need for customer research

questions.explanation: Measured results confirm or reject hypotheses and suggest new ones, which go into the next round of exploration. Research still continues. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team reports success because its feature was released on time and on budget. What is missing?

options.text: Evidence that the expected benefit was delivered
A larger budget for the next feature in the PI
A longer list of the defects that were fixed
A note of the team members who worked on it

questions.explanation: In SAFe, on time and on budget describe delivery; success means the benefit hypothesis was met. The measure activity supplies that evidence. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which tool lets a team gather results from selected users before everyone sees a change?

options.text: A longer code review
A targeted feature toggle
A full-scope user manual
A larger staging environment

questions.explanation: Targeted toggles expose a feature to a chosen group, so its measures can be collected before everyone sees it. Staging and reviews do not involve real users. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Measure”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What happens in the learn activity of Release on Demand?

options.text: Running a sales campaign for the new release
Pivot, persevere or stop; improve the pipeline
Writing a training course about the released feature
Archiving the code of the released feature

questions.explanation: Learn uses the measured results to decide the feature's future and applies lessons to the pipeline itself. It is not training or marketing. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: A feature met its hypothesis, and users ask for more of the same. What does the learn activity suggest?

options.text: Persevere and add follow-on features to the backlog
Remove the feature to test whether users miss it
Pivot to a different idea to try something new
Stop, since the hypothesis is already proved

questions.explanation: A confirmed hypothesis with demand for more supports persevering, with new features ranked in the ART backlog. Stopping or pivoting would waste a proven direction. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does the learn activity look at the pipeline as well as the feature?

options.text: Pipeline reviews replace the Inspect and Adapt event
Features cannot be judged until the pipeline is perfect
Each release shows where the pipeline is slow or fragile
The pipeline is redesigned from scratch after each release

questions.explanation: Release experience reveals delays, manual steps and weak points in the pipeline, which feed improvement work. Inspect and Adapt still runs each PI. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train learns that a released feature had no effect. Which response best fits SAFe's view of learning?

options.text: Hide the result to protect the train's reputation
Keep building the feature until it shows an effect
Treat it as useful evidence and redirect capacity
Find the team to blame for the failed feature

questions.explanation: A disproved hypothesis tells the train where not to invest, which frees capacity for better bets. Blame and hiding stop people sharing evidence. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Where does a train collect improvement items from many releases across a PI?

options.text: The portfolio's annual budget review meeting
The daily stand-up of each agile team
The System Demo held at each iteration's end
The problem-solving workshop at I&A

questions.explanation: Inspect and Adapt ends with a problem-solving workshop that turns the PI's issues into improvement backlog items. Stand-ups and demos serve other purposes. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: After several releases, a train sees the same manual approval step delay each one. What should learn produce?

options.text: A note in the release log that the delay is normal
A rule to schedule releases around the approver
A request for the approver to work longer hours
An improvement item to automate or simplify it

questions.explanation: Learning turns a repeated delay into an improvement item, such as automating or decentralising the approval. Working around it keeps the waste. Topic 6.4, lesson “6.4 · Learn”. Not checked against a public page.
